The exact timing of the Day of Judgment (“the Hour”) is known only to God; it will come suddenly and overwhelm all creation. Muḥammad has no power to benefit or harm himself except by God’s will, and is not omniscient — he is only a warner and a bringer of good tidings to those who believe.

The surah returns to the theme of human creation: God created all people from a single soul and its mate, and recounts how, when people are desperate (such as during pregnancy), they pray sincerely to God for a healthy child, but once they are blessed, some ascribe partners to God. The folly of idol worship is exposed: these false gods are powerless, unable even to help themselves, let alone their worshippers. They lack faculties and cannot respond to prayers.

Muḥammad is instructed to adopt a gentle and tolerant attitude, enjoining good and ignoring the ignorant. Should Satan incite an evil impulse, the remedy is to seek refuge in God. Those who are mindful of God gain insight immediately when tempted, while others persist in error, abetted by their “brothers” — the devils.

The surah concludes by defending the divine origin and purpose of the Qur’an. When skeptics demand new miracles, Muḥammad is reminded to say that he only follows revelation, and that the Qur’an itself is light, guidance, and mercy for believers. The surah instructs that when the Qur’an is recited, people should listen attentively to receive mercy. Remembrance of God should be done with humility and awe, not with ostentation. The angels, who are near to God, are not too proud to worship Him; they glorify and prostrate before Him.

In summary, Sūrah al-Aʿrāf is a sweeping discourse on divine guidance and human accountability. It combines theological principles (God’s sovereignty, the nature of revelation, the afterlife) with moral exhortations (justice, honesty, humility), legal and ritual guidance (worship, dietary laws, modesty), and historical narratives (stories of the prophets and their peoples). The surah repeatedly warns against the arrogance and heedlessness that led past nations to destruction, while offering hope, mercy, and guidance to those who sincerely repent and follow God’s path. It paints a vivid picture of the afterlife, with its divisions between the blessed and the damned, and urges all people to heed the message of God sent through His final messenger, Muḥammad, for the ultimate success in this life and the next.

Sūrah al-Anfāl (“The Spoils of War”) is a Medinan chapter of the Qur’an, revealed in the aftermath of the Battle of Badr, the first major military confrontation between the early Muslims and the pagan Quraysh of Mecca. The Surah deals with a host of themes: the distribution of war gains, the nature of true faith, divine intervention in battle, moral and legal guidance for the Muslim community in conflict, and the differences between believers and disbelievers in this life and the next. The Surah’s core concern is to shape the nascent Muslim community’s ethical, legal, and spiritual outlook during a period of vulnerability and conflict.

The Surah opens by addressing a practical question that arose after the Battle of Badr: who has the right to the spoils of war? The answer is that ultimate authority over the spoils belongs to Allah and His Messenger, and the community is instructed to fear God, resolve disputes among themselves, and obey divine and prophetic guidance as a mark of true belief. This sets the tone for the Surah: material matters must be guided by spiritual discipline, communal harmony, and obedience to higher authority.

The Surah then defines the characteristics of true believers: those whose hearts are humbled when God is mentioned, whose faith increases when they hear His revelations, who rely on their Lord, keep up the ritual prayer, and spend charitably from what they have been given. These qualities are presented as the criteria for spiritual success, promising believers elevated status, forgiveness, and generous provision from God.

The narrative shifts to recount the events leading to the Battle of Badr. God reminds the Prophet and the community that their expedition was guided by truth, even though some within the group were reluctant and fearful, disputing the necessity of battle as if they were being driven to their deaths. The text recalls that the Muslims were hoping to encounter the less-defended Meccan trade caravan, but God’s intention was to confront the armed Quraysh force to establish truth and expose falsehood, despite the believers’ initial hesitance.

Divine intervention is emphasized: when the Muslims prayed for help, God promised to reinforce them with a thousand angels, a pledge meant to reassure rather than to guarantee victory through supernatural means. Ultimately, victory comes from God alone, who is all-powerful and wise. The Surah also recalls the divine signs during the battle: a sleep that overcame the Muslims as a sign of security, rain sent to cleanse and strengthen them, and God’s command to the angels to support the believers and terrify the enemy. This establishes that, in Islamic theology, historical outcomes are shaped by both human effort and divine will.

The Surah warns against cowardice and disobedience in battle, stating that turning away from the fighting, except as a tactical maneuver, brings God’s anger and the threat of Hell. It is God alone who grants victory or defeat; even when the Prophet threw dust at the enemy, it was God’s will that determined the outcome. These reminders reinforce the idea that God tests believers through conflict and that the ultimate power lies with Him.

A warning is issued to the Meccan disbelievers: they had sought a decisive outcome and received it at Badr, suffering defeat. If they cease hostilities, it is better for them; if they persist, God will again support the believers regardless of the enemy’s numbers. The believers are urged to obey God and His Messenger, avoiding the hollow claim of having “heard” without sincere acceptance. The worst creatures, the Surah states, are those who are spiritually deaf and dumb, refusing to use reason or heed the message.

The text calls on the believers to respond to God’s call, which brings true life, and warns that God stands between a person and their own heart—a reminder of divine control over human intentions. The community is cautioned to fear collective trials or tribulations (fitnah), which may afflict the innocent alongside the guilty. This is a call to vigilance and communal responsibility, as well as a reminder of God’s severe punishment for those who transgress.

The Surah recalls the vulnerable state of the early Muslims: few in number, oppressed, and living in fear until God provided them sanctuary, victory, and blessings as a reason for gratitude. Believers are forbidden from betraying God, His Messenger, or one another’s trusts. Wealth and children are described as tests, not ends in themselves, while God’s reward is greater and more lasting.

God promises that those who are mindful of Him will be granted a “criterion” (furqān)—a means to discern right from wrong—as well as forgiveness and bounty. The Surah revisits the plot by the Meccan leaders to imprison, kill, or expel the Prophet, affirming that while humans scheme, God’s plan ultimately prevails. The Meccan disbelievers, when confronted with the Qur’an, dismissed it as old tales and even challenged God to send punishment if the message was true, but God refrained from punishing them while the Prophet was among them or while some still sought forgiveness.

The text criticizes the Meccans for barring access to the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Ḥarām) and for their distorted forms of worship (whistling and clapping), asserting that only the righteous are true custodians of the sanctuary. Their wealth, spent to oppose God’s cause, will become a source of regret and will not save them from defeat or the ultimate gathering in Hell.

God’s intent in these trials is to separate the wicked from the good, ultimately consigning the former to Hell. However, the Surah offers an olive branch: if the disbelievers cease their hostility, past offenses will be forgiven; if they persist, they will meet the same fate as earlier rebellious peoples. The Muslims are instructed to fight until oppression and religious persecution (fitnah) are eliminated and worship is devoted to God alone, but if the enemy ceases hostilities, God is fully aware of their actions.

The Surah institutes a rule for distributing war gains: one-fifth of the spoils belong to God, the Messenger, the Prophet’s kin, orphans, the needy, and stranded travelers, after affirming faith in God, the Prophet, and the events of Badr (“the Day of the Criterion”). This sets an ethical system for wealth gained in conflict, balancing spiritual accountability with social welfare.

The Surah provides a detailed recollection of the circumstances at Badr: the positions of the two armies and the trade caravan, God’s orchestration of the encounter, and the psychological factors at play. God made the enemy appear few in the Prophet’s dream and in the eyes of the Muslims, preventing fear and hesitation, and vice versa, so that the encounter would unfold as divinely destined, making faith and disbelief clear on the basis of evidence.

Practical advice is given for conduct in battle: stand firm, remember God, avoid disputes that lead to weakness, and cultivate patience. The Muslims are warned not to behave arrogantly or for show, as the Meccan army did, nor to be swayed by Satan’s temptations. The narrative recalls how Satan encouraged the enemy but abandoned them at the moment of confrontation, claiming to fear God and His punishment.

The Surah exposes the attitudes of hypocrites and skeptics within the Muslim ranks who mocked the believers’ trust in God. The text asserts that those who place their faith in God will find Him mighty and wise, while the fate of the disbelievers is vividly depicted: at death, the angels strike their faces and backs, announcing the punishment of Hell as a direct consequence of their actions and disbelief. This fate is likened to that of Pharaoh and earlier peoples who denied God’s signs.

The Surah emphasizes the principle that God does not remove a blessing from a people unless they themselves become corrupt. The destruction of Pharaoh and his people is cited as a historical warning. The worst creatures, it reiterates, are those who persistently break treaties and refuse to honor their commitments, displaying no fear of God.

Muslims are instructed about how to deal with those who repeatedly break treaties: if they gain the upper hand, they should act in a way that deters others from similar betrayal. However, if betrayal is suspected, the treaty should be formally annulled rather than secretly violated, upholding integrity even in conflict. The disbelievers are warned not to imagine they can escape God’s justice.

The Surah instructs the community to prepare as much as possible for defense—material strength and readiness serve to deter enemies and reassure allies. However, the use of force is not unconditional: if the enemy inclines toward peace, Muslims are to accept it and place their trust in God. Even if there is suspicion of treachery, God’s support is sufficient, as He brought unity to the believers—a unity that human means alone could never have achieved.

The Prophet is assured that God is enough for him and those who follow him. The believers are urged to steadfastness in battle, with the assurance that a small group of patient and resolute Muslims can, by God’s permission, overcome much larger forces. This was initially set at a ratio of one to ten but later eased to one to two, acknowledging the community’s human limitations.

An important legal and ethical issue is addressed: it is not proper for a prophet to take prisoners of war before a decisive victory in battle, as worldly gain should not outweigh the pursuit of justice and truth. The Muslims are reminded that their desire for ransom and material benefit was secondary to God’s purpose. However, God permitted them to benefit from the war gains as lawful, while urging them to be conscious of His mercy and forgiveness.

The treatment of prisoners is discussed: the Prophet is to assure captives that if they show sincerity, God will reward them with something better and forgive their past. If, however, they plan betrayal, they will face the consequences as those before them did. This underscores the Islamic principle of offering mercy and opportunities for repentance, while maintaining vigilance against treachery.

The Surah concludes with broader guidance for the organization of the Muslim community. Those who believed, emigrated (made hijrah), and struggled with their wealth and lives for God’s cause, along with those who gave them refuge and assistance, are declared to be allies. Those who believe but do not emigrate have no claim to protection until they do so, except in cases where there is a treaty with others. The disbelievers, by contrast, are united in alliance against the believers. Failure to maintain unity among the Muslims would result in widespread oppression and corruption.

The Surah closes by affirming that all those who join the community of faith, emigrate, and struggle in God’s cause share in this spiritual fraternity, but blood relations retain priority in matters of inheritance, according to God’s decree. The Surah ends by reminding readers that God is all-knowing and fully aware of all matters, underscoring the comprehensive nature of divine justice and guidance.

In summary, Sūrah al-Anfāl is a multifaceted chapter that addresses the realities of conflict, communal ethics, spiritual states, and practical law in the formative period of the Muslim community. It weaves together historical narrative, legal rulings, spiritual exhortation, and eschatological warning to construct a coherent vision of a God-conscious, disciplined, and united society, where success in both this world and the next is rooted in faith, integrity, and obedience to God and His Messenger.

Sūrah at-Tawbah (The Repentance) is a Medinan surah revealed late in the Prophet Muhammad’s (peace be upon him) mission, during a time when the Muslim community in Madinah had grown strong but still faced threats from the surrounding polytheist tribes and the Byzantine Empire. This surah is unique in that it is the only surah in the Qur’an that does not begin with the phrase “Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim” (“In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful”), which many scholars interpret as reflecting its stern and declarative tone.

The surah begins by announcing a clear disavowal from Allah and His Messenger of all treaties with the polytheists who had repeatedly broken agreements with the Muslims. These groups are given a four-month reprieve to move freely in the land, but are warned that they cannot escape Allah’s power and that disgrace will befall the disbelievers. The declaration is made during the “greater pilgrimage” (Hajj al-Akbar), marking a public and irrevocable shift in relations. Those disbelievers who had not violated their treaties and had not aided in hostility against the Muslims are exempted from this revocation; their treaties will be honored until their terms expire. Allah emphasizes that He loves those who act righteously and faithfully uphold their commitments.

After the passing of the sacred months, the surah commands that the Muslims must confront those hostile polytheists: if they do not repent and embrace Islam, the Muslims are to fight them as a matter of justice and defense, but if the polytheists repent, establish prayer, and pay the obligatory charity (zakāh), they are to be left in peace. Even in conflict, mercy is emphasized: if any polytheist seeks protection, the Muslims must grant it and ensure his safe passage, so that he may have the opportunity to hear Allah’s message. The surah stresses that the Muslims are only to fight those who have shown enmity and broken treaties, while upholding justice and integrity toward those who remain faithful.

The surah questions the logic of ongoing treaties with polytheists who have proven treacherous. Historical experiences are cited: if these groups gained the upper hand, they would show no regard for kinship or agreements. Their outward words are deceptive, and they have exchanged Allah’s guidance for fleeting worldly gain, actively turning others away from the path of God. The surah calls for believers to fight the “leaders of disbelief” if they break their oaths and attack Islam, highlighting that such actions are necessary not for aggression, but to protect the community and its faith from relentless hostility.

The surah reminds the believers that their loyalty must be to Allah, His Messenger, and the believing community above all else. Even family ties must not outweigh commitment to the faith if relatives choose disbelief over belief. The believers are challenged: if they love family, wealth, or status more than Allah and striving in His cause, they should expect Allah’s decisive judgment. This is illustrated by reference to past victories, such as the Battle of Hunayn, where reliance on numbers failed but God’s support and the descent of angels ensured success. The surah emphasizes that Allah alone grants victory, and that repentance and forgiveness are always possible for those who turn back after error.

The surah then addresses the status of the holy sanctuary, al-Masjid al-Ḥarām in Makkah, declaring that the polytheists are no longer permitted to approach it after that year. This ruling is not to impoverish the Muslims, who may fear the loss of trade, but they are assured that Allah will provide for them. The surah also introduces the concept of jizyah, a tax paid by non-Muslims (specifically, People of the Book—Jews and Christians) living under Muslim protection, in exchange for exemption from military service and as acknowledgement of the new societal order. The surah critiques the beliefs of Jews and Christians, including the claims about ‘Uzayr (Ezra) and Jesus being sons of God, and their tendency to follow religious leaders to the point of attributing to them divine authority. The core message is that worship belongs only to Allah, and all innovations or distortions in belief are to be rejected.

A warning is given against religious leaders and monks who exploit their followers and amass wealth without using it in righteous ways. Those who hoard riches are threatened with severe punishment in the hereafter, when their wealth will become a means of torment. The surah reiterates the sanctity of the four sacred months and condemns manipulative practices such as “postponing” (nasi’), in which pre-Islamic Arabs would shift the sacred months to suit their interests, making lawful what Allah had forbidden. Such manipulation is described as an increase in disbelief and further evidence of the corruption that Islam came to correct.

The surah calls the believing community to readiness for sacrifice, asking why some hesitate to go forth in Allah’s cause. It warns that clinging to the comforts of earthly life over the hereafter is a profound error, and if the Muslims do not respond to the call, Allah can replace them with others. The migration of the Prophet Muhammad and Abu Bakr from Makkah to Madinah is referenced as an example of Allah’s support in the darkest hour, when divine tranquility and unseen forces (angels) ensured the Prophet’s safety.

The surah then addresses the issue of hypocrisy within the community, particularly during the expedition of Tabūk, which required great sacrifice. Some people sought excuses to avoid participation, showing a lack of faith and commitment. The surah distinguishes between those whose hearts are firm and those whose doubts and reluctance expose their insincerity. It is made clear that those who are genuinely unable to participate due to weakness, illness, or lack of resources are not to be blamed. The surah criticizes those who are quick to complain about the distribution of charity or who only contribute grudgingly, and it discusses the correct recipients of zakāh: the poor, the needy, those employed to collect it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, for freeing slaves, for those in debt, for the cause of Allah, and for travelers in need.

The surah highlights the hypocrites’ duplicity: they criticize the Prophet, mock the believers, and swear false oaths, but their real motivation is fear and self-interest. They are warned of a painful punishment, and the Prophet is told not to pray for their forgiveness, as their persistent disbelief and mockery have sealed their fate. The surah contrasts the hypocrites with the true believers, who support one another, strive for good, and are promised Allah’s mercy and eternal gardens.

The surah recalls the fate of earlier communities destroyed for their arrogance and disbelief: the people of Nūḥ (Noah), ʿĀd, Thamūd, Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Midian, and the “overturned towns” (Sodom and Gomorrah). These examples serve as a stern reminder that those who reject their prophets and persist in wrongdoing ultimately destroy themselves. The surah also encourages the Muslims to be firm against the disbelievers and hypocrites, and warns that their end is Hell.

The surah describes the different attitudes of the Bedouin Arabs: some are hard-hearted and resistant to religious discipline, while others are sincere in their faith and charitable in their actions. Those who are first in faith (the Muhājirūn—emigrants from Makkah, and the Anṣār—helpers in Madinah) and those who follow them with sincerity are praised and promised Allah’s pleasure and eternal reward.

The surah details how some people mixed good deeds with bad and acknowledges their repentance, instructing the Prophet to accept their charity as a means of purification. Others’ fate is left to Allah’s judgment. It also describes a group of hypocrites who built a mosque not for righteousness, but to cause harm and division. The Prophet is told never to stand in this mosque; the only mosque worthy of his presence is one founded on piety from the very beginning (considered by many to refer to Masjid Qubā’). The difference between building on righteousness and building on shaky or corrupt foundations is illustrated with the parable of a building on a collapsing cliff.

The surah then powerfully asserts that Allah has “purchased” the lives and wealth of the believers in exchange for Paradise, describing the qualities of those who attain this status: they are repentant, worshipful, praiseful, active in good works, and uphold Allah’s boundaries. The Prophet and the believers are told it is not appropriate to ask forgiveness for polytheists, even if they are close relatives, once it is clear that they are destined for Hell, as exemplified by Ibrāhīm’s disassociation from his father after learning of his enmity to Allah.

The surah reaffirms Allah’s dominion over life and death, and His exclusive power to guide or allow people to go astray only after providing clear warning. It recalls Allah’s mercy in forgiving the Prophet, the Muhājirūn, and the Anṣār after a moment of weakness during the “hour of difficulty” (the expedition to Tabūk), and also the sincere repentance of the three companions who were boycotted due to their failure to join the campaign. Their anguish and Allah’s eventual acceptance of their repentance is described as an example of divine mercy.

The surah underscores the importance of solidarity among the Muslims, stating that it is not proper for the people of Madinah or the neighboring Bedouins to lag behind the Prophet or prefer their own comfort over his cause. Every action, hardship, or expense in the cause of Allah is registered as a righteous deed, and no effort is wasted. However, the surah also balances activism with the need for learning: not everyone is required to go forth to battle at once, as some must remain to study and teach the faith, ensuring the community’s religious understanding.

The surah continues with instructions to fight those neighboring disbelievers who are openly hostile, emphasizing that the believers must be resolute and that Allah is with those who are righteous. The surah draws attention to the different reactions to revelation: true believers find their faith increased, while those with diseased hearts only become more entrenched in their opposition. The hypocrites, exposed by the revelations, make excuses and seek to avoid accountability, but Allah’s judgment will ultimately prevail.

The closing verses describe the Prophet’s deep concern for his community and his kindness and mercy toward the believers. The surah ends with a reminder that, should people turn away, Allah alone is sufficient for the Prophet, and that ultimate reliance and trust must be placed in the Lord of the Throne, who alone governs all affairs.

In summary, Sūrah at-Tawbah is a comprehensive and uncompromising call to faithfulness, honesty, sacrifice, and solidarity within the Muslim community. It addresses the realities of conflict, hypocrisy, and religious obligation, setting boundaries for relations with disbelievers and hypocrites, and providing clear principles for justice, forgiveness, and the pursuit of Allah’s pleasure. It is both a stern warning and an invitation to sincere repentance, closing with a reaffirmation of trust in Allah’s wisdom and mercy.

Sūrah Yūnus (Chapter of Jonah) is a Meccan surah, revealed during a time of mounting opposition to the Prophet Muḥammad’s (peace be upon him) message. It opens by highlighting that its verses are from a wise, divinely-revealed Book, immediately establishing the authority and purpose of the Qur’an as guidance for humanity.

The surah addresses the initial amazement and skepticism of the people: how could God send revelation to a human being from among themselves? The Prophet is instructed to warn humanity and give glad tidings to the believers of special favor with their Lord. However, the disbelievers dismiss the message as sorcery, reflecting a recurring theme of rejection by those attached to their traditions and status quo.

The surah grounds its message in the sovereignty of Allah (God), who created the heavens and earth in six days and then established control over the universe. He alone manages creation and allows no intercession except by His permission. This passage calls people to worship Allah exclusively, urging reflection on His power and mercy.

The surah emphasizes that all people will ultimately return to Allah, who will resurrect creation and judge with perfect justice. Those who believe and do good will be rewarded, while those who reject faith will face painful punishment symbolized by scalding water. This introduces the central eschatological theme: the reality of resurrection, reward, and punishment.

The text draws attention to natural signs: the sun and moon, their roles in marking time, and the cycles of night and day. These are described not simply as physical phenomena, but as purposeful signs for people who reflect—reminding humanity of the Creator’s wisdom and urging awe and gratitude.

The surah then contrasts two types of people: those content with worldly life who neglect the hereafter, and those attentive to God’s signs. The former are warned that their ultimate fate will be the Fire, a consequence of their heedlessness. The latter—who believe and act righteously—are promised divine guidance, eternal gardens beneath which rivers flow, and a life of peace, praise, and gratitude in Paradise (Jannah).

The narrative highlights human inconsistency: when afflicted, people desperately pray to God for relief, but when the hardship is lifted, many return to heedlessness and self-reliance. This pattern is critiqued as self-delusion, a recurring theme in the Qur’an’s analysis of human psychology.

Historical precedent is invoked: past generations who wronged themselves were destroyed after rejecting clear proofs brought by their prophets. The current generation has been made successors on earth; their actions are a test to see how they will behave, echoing the Qur’anic motif of history as moral instruction.

When the Qur’an is recited with clear evidence, those who reject the hereafter demand either a different revelation or changes to it. The Prophet is told to assert his lack of authority to alter revelation and to warn of severe consequences for disobedience. He appeals to their knowledge of his lifelong honesty before prophethood as further evidence of his sincerity.

The surah critiques the practice of associating partners with God, especially the belief that idols can intercede with Allah. It challenges the logic and legitimacy of these claims, emphasizing that only God has knowledge of the unseen and that such associations are baseless fabrications.

The unity of humanity is noted: all people were once a single community, but differences arose. Ultimate judgment over these disputes is deferred only because of God’s decree. The disbelievers demand miraculous signs, but they are told that the unseen and the timing of signs are God’s prerogative. The Prophet is instructed to wait patiently along with them, leaving the matter to divine wisdom.

The surah observes that people often respond to God’s mercy with ingratitude, conspiring against His signs after being relieved from adversity. It warns that God’s response is swifter and more thorough than their plots, as everything is recorded by angels.

A vivid parable is presented: travelers at sea, when threatened by storms, pray sincerely to God for rescue, vowing gratitude. Yet once saved, many revert to injustice and heedlessness. The surah points out that such injustice only harms the perpetrators themselves, as earthly life is fleeting and all will return to God for reckoning.

The temporary nature of worldly life is likened to rain that produces lush vegetation, which can be destroyed overnight by God’s command, leaving no trace. This illustrates the fragility of material achievements and the need for thoughtful reflection on existence’s purpose.

Allah’s invitation to the “Home of Peace” (Paradise) is underscored, as is His exclusive authority to guide people to the straight path. Those who do good are promised the best reward and even “extra”—interpreted by tradition as the ultimate pleasure of seeing God—with no fear or humiliation. In contrast, evildoers face equivalent punishment and disgrace, likened to darkness covering their faces, and are destined for the Fire.

The surah describes the Day of Judgment, when idolaters and their supposed “partners” will be gathered and separated. The so-called partners will disclaim any knowledge of being worshipped, and God’s testimony will expose the truth. On that day, each soul will face the consequences of its deeds, and all false beliefs will vanish.

The Prophet is challenged to question the idolaters: Who provides sustenance, controls life and death, and manages the universe? Even the idolaters admit it is God, yet they persist in associating others with Him. The surah points out the inconsistency of following error after acknowledging the truth.

The Qur’an’s divine origin is defended: it could not have been produced by anyone but Allah. It confirms prior scriptures and clarifies earlier revelation. The disbelievers are invited to produce a surah like it if they claim it is fabricated, a challenge they cannot meet.

The surah explains why people reject revelation: they deny what they do not fully understand, just as earlier peoples denied their prophets. Some will believe, others not. The Prophet is instructed to separate himself from the deeds of the rejecters, emphasizing personal responsibility and the limits of his mission.

The surah uses metaphors of blindness and deafness to illustrate that some people, despite hearing or seeing the message, are unwilling to understand or accept it. Ultimately, God does not wrong anyone; people wrong themselves by their choices.

The brevity of worldly life is emphasized: on the Day of Judgment, it will seem as if people lived only an hour. Those who denied resurrection will realize their loss too late. The Prophet is reassured that whether he lives to see the promised judgment or not, God is the ultimate witness and judge.

Every nation has been sent a messenger, and when the messenger comes, judgment is rendered with perfect justice. The surah addresses the skeptics who impatiently demand the fulfillment of divine promises, reminding them that God’s timing is fixed and unavoidable.

People are warned that regret will be useless once punishment arrives. Wealth and power will not be able to ransom anyone from God’s judgment. The reality of the resurrection and God’s ownership of all things is affirmed.

The surah calls humanity to rejoice in the guidance and mercy found in revelation, which is described as healing and instruction for the heart. This spiritual bounty is far superior to material wealth.

The surah criticizes those who make up their own rules about what is lawful or unlawful regarding God’s provisions, challenging them to show divine authorization for such claims. It warns that inventing lies about God leads to severe consequences in the hereafter.

God’s comprehensive knowledge is highlighted: nothing escapes His awareness, not even an atom’s weight in the heavens or earth. Every action is recorded in a “clear register,” underlining the meticulousness of divine accountability.

The “allies of God” (awliyāʾ)—those who believe and are mindful of Him—are assured of security and glad tidings in both this life and the next. This unchanging promise is described as the greatest attainment, offering comfort to the Prophet amid opposition.

The surah reassures the Prophet not to be saddened by the speech of the disbelievers, as true honor belongs to God alone. Most people, however, are ungrateful for God’s bounty and misled by false assumptions.

The surah rejects the claim that God has taken a son—an allusion to certain pre-Islamic and Christian beliefs—declaring God utterly self-sufficient and above such needs. Asserting things about God without knowledge is condemned as a serious falsehood.

The fate of those who invent lies about God is clear: temporary enjoyment in this world followed by severe punishment in the hereafter. This underscores the seriousness of misrepresenting God and the ultimate futility of such actions.

The stories of past prophets are recounted as moral lessons. The narrative of Nūḥ (Noah) is presented: despite his persistence and reliance on God, his people rejected him. Noah disavowed any worldly reward, seeking only God’s acceptance. When they denied him, God saved him and his followers while destroying the rejecters, making them lessons for future generations.

The surah summarizes the pattern of prophetic history: after Noah, successive prophets faced similar responses of denial. Moses (Mūsā) and Aaron (Hārūn) were sent to Pharaoh (Firʿawn) and his elite, who dismissed their message as magic and clung to ancestral traditions. Pharaoh challenged Moses with magicians, but God exposed their tricks and upheld the truth.

Moses’ followers were few, mostly young people, due to fear of Pharaoh’s tyranny. Moses urged his people to trust in God, and they prayed for rescue from oppression and not to be a test for the wrongdoers. God instructed them to maintain their faith and establish prayer, even under threat.

Moses prayed for Pharaoh’s destruction, asking God to harden their hearts so they would not repent until punishment came. God granted this, and the final confrontation unfolded with the miraculous parting of the sea. Pharaoh, facing death, declared belief too late. His body was preserved as a sign for future generations, illustrating both the certainty of divine retribution and the limits of last-minute repentance.

The Israelites were then settled in a good land and provided with blessings. However, they too fell into disputes after receiving knowledge, foreshadowing the persistent human tendency to divide even after receiving guidance. Final judgment between them is deferred to the Day of Resurrection.

The Prophet is assured that the truth of his revelation is certain, and he is urged never to doubt or join those who reject God’s signs. The text insists that some, despite every sign, will never believe until they see punishment, demonstrating the finality of God’s decree upon persistent rejecters.

The unique story of the people of Yūnus (Jonah) is mentioned: unlike other nations, when they believed in time, God lifted the punishment from them and allowed them to enjoy life for a period. This exception highlights both God’s mercy and the importance of timely repentance.

The surah reflects on the nature of faith: belief is ultimately by God’s leave, and no one can be compelled to believe. God allows those who reject faith without thought to remain in spiritual impurity, and no sign or warning is effective for those who refuse to engage their reason.

The surah closes with a series of exhortations and summaries. The Prophet is instructed to declare his detachment from idol worship and to affirm his exclusive devotion to God, the One who gives life and death. He is told to direct himself steadfastly to true religion, avoiding all association of partners with God.

The surah warns that only God can remove adversity or grant good, and He extends His mercy as He wills. The Prophet’s role is to deliver the truth; each person’s guidance or misguidance affects only themselves. The Prophet is not a controller over people, but a conveyor of revelation.

Finally, the surah counsels patient perseverance for the Prophet: to follow revelation, endure opposition, and await God’s ultimate judgment, for He is the most just of judges. This concluding note encapsulates the surah’s themes of divine sovereignty, human accountability, the inevitability of judgment, and the Prophet’s unwavering commitment to truth.

Sūrah Hūd opens by affirming the divine origin and precision of the Qur’ān. It describes the scripture as one whose verses are both perfected and detailed, coming from Allah, the All-Wise and All-Aware. The message is delivered through a messenger whose fundamental call is to worship Allah alone, warning people against idolatry and promising glad tidings to those who obey. The Surah urges people to seek forgiveness from their Lord and to repent, promising good provision and rewards for those who do good, while warning of a great punishment for those who turn away. It emphasizes the inevitability of returning to Allah, who has power over all things.

The Surah addresses the tendency of some people to conceal their disbelief and opposition, thinking they can hide their true feelings and intentions even from the Prophet. However, it asserts that Allah knows everything—what is hidden and what is revealed, and even the secrets of the hearts. It further states that Allah is responsible for the sustenance of every creature on earth, fully aware of their whereabouts and destinies; everything is recorded in a clear register.

Moving to the creation of the universe, the Surah states that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days while His Throne was upon water, all as a test for humankind to see who performs best in deeds. The idea of resurrection is introduced, noting that when the Prophet announces life after death, the disbelievers dismiss it as magic. When punishment is delayed, they question its postponement, but the Surah warns that when it finally arrives, it will be inescapable, and those who mocked it will be overwhelmed.

The Surah explores the fickle nature of human beings. When blessed with mercy and then tested with hardship, people often become despairing and ungrateful. Conversely, when hardship is lifted, they become boastful. However, those who are patient and do good deeds are promised forgiveness and a great reward.

The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) is addressed directly, acknowledging the heavy burden of delivering the message in the face of opposition and mockery. The Surah reassures him that he is only a warner, not responsible for people’s demands for miracles or treasures. The Qur’ān’s authenticity is defended by challenging skeptics to produce ten chapters like it, calling on anyone they can for help. Their inability to do so confirms the Qur’ān’s divine origin. The Surah distinguishes between those who seek only worldly gain, who will be fully repaid in this world but will have nothing but the Fire in the Hereafter, and those who follow clear evidence and believe in the divine scriptures, whose reward is Paradise.

The Surah then denounces those who invent lies about Allah, warning that they will face public disgrace and divine curse. Such people lead others astray, distort the truth, and reject the Hereafter. They will receive multiplied punishment and will be utterly lost, while the believers who humble themselves to their Lord will enjoy eternal happiness in Paradise. The Surah uses the analogy of the blind and deaf versus the seeing and hearing to illustrate the difference between the misguided and the guided.

The narrative section of the Surah begins with the story of Nūḥ (Noah), who is sent as a clear warner to his people, calling them to worship Allah alone and warning of a painful punishment. The leaders of his people dismiss him as just an ordinary man and claim that only the lowliest among them follow him. They accuse him of lying and demand immediate punishment if he is truthful. Noah responds by reaffirming his sincerity, clarifying he does not ask for payment, and refusing to drive away the humble believers. He disclaims any supernatural powers or knowledge of the unseen, stressing that only Allah knows His servants’ hearts.

Noah’s people persist in their rejection and ridicule, demanding the threatened punishment. Allah informs Noah that only those already faithful will believe, and instructs him to build the Ark under divine guidance, forbidding him from pleading for the doomed. As Noah and his followers construct the Ark, they are mocked, but Noah warns that the truth will soon become clear. When the divine command arrives, the flood begins, and Noah is instructed to take pairs of creatures and the believers aboard. A poignant moment occurs when Noah’s own son refuses to join them, seeking refuge on a mountain, but is lost to the flood. The Ark comes to rest on Mount Jūdiyy, and the floodwaters subside at Allah’s command.

After the flood, Noah pleads for his son, but Allah clarifies that true kinship is based on righteousness, not blood, and that Noah’s son was unrighteous. Noah seeks forgiveness for his mistake and is reassured, being told to disembark in peace and blessings, though future generations may still go astray. The Surah notes that these are revelations of the unseen given to Muhammad, urging him to remain patient, as the ultimate outcome belongs to the righteous.

The Surah then recounts the story of the people of ʿĀd and their Prophet Hūd. Hūd calls his people to worship Allah alone, seeking no reward except from his Creator. He promises prosperity if they repent and warns of punishment if they persist in idolatry. His people, however, demand miraculous evidence and accuse him of madness. Hūd confidently asserts his reliance on Allah, declaring their threats powerless, and warns that if they turn away, Allah will replace them with another people. When the punishment comes, Hūd and his followers are saved, while the arrogant ʿĀd are destroyed and cursed in both this world and the next.

The narrative moves to the people of Thamūd and their Prophet Ṣāliḥ. Ṣāliḥ urges his people to worship Allah, reminding them of their origins and Allah’s blessings. The people, skeptical and attached to ancestral traditions, demand a miracle, which Allah provides in the form of a she-camel. Ṣāliḥ warns them not to harm her, but they defy him and kill the camel, sealing their fate. He warns of impending doom, and after three days, a devastating blast destroys the wrongdoers, leaving their homes desolate as if they had never prospered. Ṣāliḥ and the believers are saved from disgrace.

The Surah then recounts the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and his guests, who are angels in disguise. Abraham welcomes them and offers food, but is unsettled when they do not eat. The angels reveal their mission—to the people of Lūṭ (Lot)—and bring good news of the birth of Isaac and, after him, Jacob. Abraham’s wife, astonished at the news due to her old age, is reassured by the angels of Allah’s power. Abraham then pleads for the people of Lūṭ, but is told that the punishment is certain.

The angels proceed to Lūṭ, who is distressed by their arrival. The people of the city, known for their persistent immorality, besiege his house, demanding access to his guests. Lūṭ tries to dissuade them, offering his daughters (interpreted as a plea for lawful marriage), but they persist in their evil. Feeling powerless, Lūṭ is reassured by the angels of his safety and instructed to leave with his family at night, except his wife, who will share in the punishment. The city is then destroyed by being turned upside down and pelted with stones, marking an end for the wrongdoers.

The story of Shuʿayb and the people of Madyan follows. Shuʿayb calls his people to worship Allah and to be honest in business, warning them against economic corruption and exploitation. He urges them to repent, promising that lawful provision from Allah is far better. The people question whether his prayers really justify abandoning their traditions and economic practices, and they threaten him despite his family’s protection. Shuʿayb affirms his sincerity and warns of a fate similar to earlier destroyed peoples. When the divine command comes, Shuʿayb and the believers are saved, while a mighty blast destroys the wrongdoers.

The Surah then references the story of Mūsā (Moses), who is sent with signs and clear authority to Firʿawn (Pharaoh) and his elite. Pharaoh’s people follow his misguided leadership, leading them to destruction in both this world and the next. Pharaoh will lead his people into the Fire on the Day of Resurrection, and they are followed by a curse for their evil.

The Surah summarizes these narratives as lessons, noting that some of the destroyed towns remain standing while others have vanished. It emphasizes that Allah never wronged these peoples; rather, they wronged themselves by clinging to false gods that failed to help them. The Surah stresses the severity of Allah’s punishment when He seizes a wrongdoing community, and it points to the Day of Judgment as a time when all humanity will be gathered and the ultimate destinies of the wretched and the prosperous will be decided.

On that Day, no one will speak except by Allah’s permission. The wretched will be consigned to the Fire, experiencing perpetual suffering, while the prosperous will reside eternally in Jannah (Paradise), enjoying uninterrupted blessings. Allah’s will is supreme, and His decrees are final.

The Surah addresses the Prophet, reassuring him not to doubt the persistence of disbelief and idolatry among the polytheists. It reminds that divisions existed even among those who received previous scriptures, like Moses’ followers. Every individual will be fully compensated for their deeds, as Allah is fully aware of all actions.

The Surah concludes with a set of guidance and exhortations. The Prophet and the believers are urged to remain steadfast on the straight path, avoiding excess and wrongdoing. They are warned not to incline toward oppressors, lest they share their fate. The Surah emphasizes the importance of regular prayer, particularly at the two ends of the day and at night, teaching that good deeds erase bad deeds. Patience is praised, with the assurance that Allah never wastes the reward of the righteous.

The Surah reflects on why so few among past generations actively forbade corruption, noting that only a small number were saved, while most pursued luxury and ended up as wrongdoers. Allah would not destroy a community unjustly if its people were reformers. The Surah discusses the diversity of humanity and the reality of differing beliefs, explaining that universal agreement was not Allah’s will, and that mercy is reserved for those whom Allah chooses, while Hell will be filled with those who persist in evil.

The Surah makes clear that the stories of the prophets serve to strengthen the heart and provide truth, guidance, and reminders for believers. The Prophet is instructed to tell the disbelievers to do as they will, for both sides will see the consequences. All matters of the unseen belong to Allah, and ultimately, everyone will return to Him. The Surah finishes by instructing to worship and rely on Allah, who is fully aware of all actions, thus closing with a reminder of accountability and trust in the divine.

Sūrah Yūsuf (Joseph) opens by declaring that its verses are from a clear, understandable Book that has been sent down in the Arabic language so people can grasp its meaning. It emphasizes that what follows is “the best of stories,” revealed to Prophet Muḥammad, who had no prior knowledge of its details. This sets a tone of both accessibility and revelation, highlighting that what is to come is not just a tale but a divinely chosen narrative with deep wisdom.

The surah begins the story of Yūsuf (Joseph) when he shares a remarkable dream with his father, Yaʿqūb (Jacob). Joseph describes seeing eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrating to him. Jacob immediately recognizes the dream's significance, cautioning his son not to tell his brothers lest they become jealous and plot against him, since Satan is a clear enemy to humanity. Jacob reassures Joseph that God will choose him, teach him the interpretation of dreams, and complete His favor upon their family, just as He did with Abraham and Isaac. This introduces the themes of divine favor, prophetic lineage, and the power of dreams as a means of revelation.

The narrative shifts to the brothers of Joseph, who express envy and resentment that their father loves Joseph and his other young brother, Binyamīn (Benjamin), more than the rest despite their own status as a larger group. Driven by jealousy, they plot to get rid of Joseph, suggesting either killing him or casting him into a distant land so their father’s attention will turn to them. One brother persuades them to instead throw Joseph into the bottom of a well, hoping travelers will find him—thus sparing his life but removing him from their midst. This passage highlights the destructive capacity of envy, family discord, and the first major test for Joseph.

The brothers convince Jacob to let Joseph accompany them by claiming they will look after him. Jacob is reluctant and fears a wolf might harm Joseph, but the brothers mock this concern and press their case. Once Joseph is with them, they carry out their plan, casting him into the well. God inspires Joseph with reassurance that he will one day confront his brothers about this incident, though they will not recognize him. The brothers return to Jacob at night, weeping and presenting Joseph’s shirt stained with false blood, claiming a wolf devoured him. Jacob, unconvinced, recognizes deception and turns to patience and trust in God’s help.

Meanwhile, a caravan passes by the well. Their water-drawer discovers Joseph and, seeing an opportunity for profit, the travelers conceal him as merchandise. They sell Joseph in Egypt for a meager price. The man who purchases Joseph (later identified as al-ʿAzīz, a high official) instructs his wife to treat Joseph kindly, hoping he will be useful or even adopted as a son. The narrative here underscores themes of providence—Joseph is moved from misfortune to opportunity, and God’s control over events is repeatedly stressed.

As Joseph matures in Egypt, God grants him wisdom and knowledge, rewarding his steadfastness and righteousness. However, Joseph faces a new trial: the wife of al-ʿAzīz attempts to seduce him. Despite her insistence, Joseph seeks refuge with God, expressing loyalty to his master and declaring that wrongdoers do not succeed. When she persists, God enables Joseph to resist, and as they struggle, she tears his shirt from behind. Her husband discovers them, and she accuses Joseph. A member of her family proposes a test: if Joseph’s shirt is torn from the front, she is truthful; if from the back, he is innocent. The shirt is torn from the back, confirming Joseph’s account. Her husband tells Joseph to overlook the matter and instructs his wife to seek forgiveness for her wrongdoing.

The incident becomes the talk of the town, with women gossiping about the wife of al-ʿAzīz and her infatuation with a slave. To prove her case, she invites these women to a banquet and presents Joseph before them. So striking is his appearance that they cut their hands in astonishment, exclaiming he is like a noble angel, not a mere man. The wife of al-ʿAzīz admits her attempt and threatens that if Joseph does not comply, he will be imprisoned. Joseph prays for God’s protection, preferring prison over succumbing to temptation. God answers his prayer and averts their plot, but despite signs of his innocence, Joseph is imprisoned for a time.

In prison, Joseph meets two young men, both troubled by dreams. One dreams of pressing wine, the other of birds eating bread from his head. They ask Joseph to interpret their dreams, recognizing his goodness. Before interpreting, Joseph explains that his ability is a gift from God, and he contrasts his monotheistic faith—following Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—with the idol worship of Egypt. He stresses God’s oneness and authority to legislate, inviting his companions to true faith. Then, he interprets the dreams: one man will serve wine again to his master (the king), while the other will be crucified and birds will eat from his head. Joseph asks the first to mention him to the king, but Satan causes the man to forget, leaving Joseph in prison for several more years.

Eventually, the king of Egypt has a perplexing dream: seven fat cows being devoured by seven thin cows, and seven green ears of grain and seven dry ones. None of his advisors can interpret it. The former prisoner recalls Joseph and recommends him. Joseph, still in prison, gives a detailed interpretation: Egypt will enjoy seven years of abundant harvests, followed by seven years of severe famine that will consume all but what is saved, and then a year of relief and abundance. The king, impressed, seeks Joseph’s release but Joseph insists on clearing his name first, asking the king to investigate the women who injured their hands.

The king questions the women, who all affirm Joseph’s innocence. The wife of al-ʿAzīz confesses her attempt to seduce him and publicly acknowledges his integrity. She adds a reflection on the human soul’s tendency toward evil, unless God shows mercy. With his reputation vindicated, Joseph is brought before the king, who offers him a high position. Joseph requests to be put in charge of Egypt’s storehouses, citing his knowledge and trustworthiness. God thus establishes Joseph in authority, allowing him to settle wherever he wishes. The surah stresses that God’s mercy is for whomever He wills and that Joseph’s reward is not lost.

As the famine strikes, people from surrounding regions—including Joseph’s brothers—come to Egypt for provisions. Joseph recognizes his brothers, but they do not recognize him. After supplying them, he requests that they bring their youngest brother (Benjamin) on their next visit, warning that they will not receive more grain otherwise. To encourage their return, Joseph instructs his servants to secretly return their payment in their bags. The brothers return home and urge Jacob to let Benjamin go with them, but Jacob is wary, referencing his earlier loss of Joseph. When the brothers discover their money has been returned, they press their case. Jacob finally agrees, securing a solemn oath from them and advising them to enter Egypt by separate gates to avoid drawing attention, though he acknowledges that only God’s decree prevails.

When the brothers return to Egypt, Joseph privately reveals his identity to Benjamin, reassuring him not to grieve over past wrongs. As they prepare to depart with supplies, Joseph orchestrates a scheme: the king’s ceremonial measuring bowl is planted in Benjamin’s bag. The brothers are accused of theft, and, as per their own customs, the penalty is that the one found with the stolen item becomes enslaved to the accuser. The bowl is found with Benjamin, and the brothers plead for leniency, citing their father’s advanced age, but Joseph refuses to punish anyone but the guilty party.

In distress, the brothers consult privately. The eldest, recalling their broken promise to Jacob, refuses to return home and instructs the others to explain the situation honestly to their father and to refer him to people in Egypt and their caravan companions if he doubts them. When they report back, Jacob again suspects foul play, shows patience, and expresses hope that God will bring all his sons back. The loss of Joseph and Benjamin intensifies Jacob’s grief, to the point where he loses his eyesight from sorrow. He insists that he only complains to God, not to them, and encourages his sons to keep searching for Joseph and Benjamin, never despairing of God’s mercy.

The brothers return to Egypt, appealing to Joseph for aid, explaining their desperation and poor supplies. Joseph then confronts them: “Do you remember what you did to Joseph and his brother when you were ignorant?” The brothers recognize him—he reveals his identity, and they admit their wrongdoing. Joseph forgives them, declaring that no blame will fall on them and assuring them of God’s mercy. He gives them his shirt to place on Jacob’s face, promising it will restore his sight, and invites the whole family to Egypt.

As the family caravan travels from Egypt, Jacob senses the scent of Joseph and announces his hope, despite skepticism from others. When the bearer of good news arrives and places Joseph’s shirt on Jacob’s face, his sight returns. Jacob reminds his sons of his trust in God’s wisdom. The brothers ask their father to pray for their forgiveness, which he promises to do.

Upon the family’s reunion in Egypt, Joseph welcomes his parents and seats them with honor. His parents and brothers bow to him in respect, fulfilling Joseph’s childhood dream. Joseph reflects on God’s favor—his release from prison, his family’s reunification, and God’s subtle, wise management of all events. He prays, acknowledging God as his ultimate Protector and asks to die as a Muslim and be joined with the righteous.

The surah then addresses Prophet Muḥammad directly. It says these are “news of the unseen,” revealed to him, and that he was not present when Joseph’s brothers plotted against him. The surah laments that most people, despite all efforts, will not believe. It assures that the Qur’an is not seeking payment but is a universal reminder. People ignore many signs in the heavens and earth, and most believe in God only while associating others with Him—a warning against polytheism.

The final verses warn that people should not feel secure from God’s punishment or the sudden coming of the Hour (the Day of Judgment). The Prophet is instructed to declare his mission: to invite to God with clear insight, following the way of monotheism, and to disavow any association of partners with God. The surah reminds listeners that previous messengers were also human beings, sent to people of settled towns, and urges people to reflect on the fate of previous communities. The ultimate success is for those who are mindful of God.

The surah closes by noting that even when messengers despaired and thought they were denied, God’s help arrived, saving those He willed and punishing the wrongdoers. It emphasizes that in the stories of the Qur’an—especially that of Joseph—there are profound lessons for people of understanding. The Qur’an is not fabricated, but a confirmation of previous revelation, a detailed explanation, and a guide and mercy for believers.

In sum, Sūrah Yūsuf is a rich, multi-layered narrative that encompasses themes of faith, patience, the destructive nature of jealousy, the trials of temptation and injustice, forgiveness, the power of dreams, the wisdom of divine providence, and the eventual triumph of truth and righteousness. It presents the story in a way meant to comfort, instruct, and warn, both for its immediate audience and for future generations.

Sūrah ar-Raʿd (“The Thunder”) opens by affirming the divine origin and truthfulness of the Qurʾān, even though most people do not believe in it. The Surah immediately draws attention to the wonders of creation as clear signs of God's existence and power: God has established the heavens without visible pillars, arranged the sun and moon in precise orbits for set periods, and manages every aspect of existence. These details are presented so that people may be certain about meeting their Lord and the reality of life after death.

The Surah continues by describing how God has spread out the earth, placed mountains and rivers, and created all fruits in pairs. It mentions that night covers the day, all as evidence for those who reflect. The diversity within the land — neighboring plots of farmland, gardens of vines and palms, some growing from the same root and watered by the same rain, yet producing fruits of varying quality — is highlighted as a sign for those who use their intellect. These observations invite people to ponder the wisdom and power of God in the natural world.

The Surah then addresses the doubts of the disbelievers, who find it inconceivable that God could resurrect them after they have become dust. This denial is identified as the root of their disbelief, and the Surah warns that such people will face severe consequences — shackles around their necks and eternal punishment in Hell. The stubbornness of the disbelievers is further illustrated by their demand for immediate punishment rather than seeking good; they ask for evil to befall them as proof, despite the fact that similar punishments have already occurred in the past. Nevertheless, God is described as both forgiving and severe in punishment, emphasizing both His mercy and justice.

Another objection raised by the disbelievers is the absence of a miraculous sign for Muḥammad. The Surah clarifies that the Prophet’s role is to warn, and that every community receives its own guide. It then shifts focus to God’s all-encompassing knowledge: He knows what every female carries in her womb, whether the pregnancy is completed or ends early, and everything is measured with precision. God’s knowledge includes both the unseen and the seen, and He is described as grand and exalted.

The Surah stresses that all human actions, whether concealed or public, are known to God. People are protected by angels who guard them by God’s command, but the key principle is that God does not change a people’s condition unless they change themselves. If God intends harm for a people, there is no one who can avert it or act as their protector besides Him. This reinforces the idea of personal responsibility and divine sovereignty.

Signs of God’s power are evident in the natural phenomena: He shows lightning which inspires both fear and hope, produces heavy clouds, and sends thunderbolts that strike as He wills. Even the thunder itself, along with the angels, glorifies God out of awe. Despite these signs, people continue to dispute about God — yet He remains severe in His power and punishment.

The Surah makes a theological point about prayer and worship: only God responds to sincere supplications, while those who call on other beings besides Him are compared to someone reaching for water from afar but never attaining it. The prayers of disbelievers are described as futile. Furthermore, everything in the heavens and the earth, including their shadows, submits to God willingly or unwillingly.

Through a series of rhetorical questions, the Surah challenges the logic of associating partners with God. It asks whether blind and seeing, or darkness and light, can be considered equal, and whether any supposed partners of God have created anything similar to His creation. The answer is that God alone is the Creator and the Supreme Authority; all other claims are baseless.

A parable is given using rain and floods: when rain falls, valleys carry water according to their capacity, and foam rises to the surface, just as when metals are purified by fire. The foam, representing falsehood, disappears, while what benefits people — symbolizing truth — remains. This example illustrates that truth ultimately endures, while falsehood fades away.

The Surah then contrasts the fate of those who respond to God’s call versus those who reject it. The faithful are promised the best reward, whereas the disbelievers, even if they possessed all the riches of the earth, could not ransom themselves from severe judgment and Hell. The Surah emphasizes that people who recognize the truth of the revelation are not equal to those who are spiritually blind; only those with real understanding take heed.

The traits of the truly mindful are described: fulfilling God’s covenant, maintaining relationships God has commanded to be maintained, fearing their Lord, and dreading the consequences of their actions. These people are patient for God’s sake, establish prayer, spend from their wealth both publicly and secretly, and respond to evil with good. Their reward is described as Paradise (Jannah), a permanent abode where they will be joined by their righteous family members, greeted by angels with words of peace and praise for their patience.

In contrast, those who break God’s covenant, sever ties that God ordered to be maintained, and cause corruption on earth will be cursed and have the worst possible destination in the afterlife. The Surah then comments on the nature of worldly provision: God alone controls who receives abundance and who faces restriction. Those who are attached to worldly life are reminded that compared to the Hereafter, this life is fleeting and insignificant.

The disbelievers persist in demanding miraculous signs, but the Surah states that God allows some people to go astray while guiding those who turn to Him. Faith brings tranquility to the heart, and the remembrance of God is the true source of inner peace. The believers who do righteous deeds are promised a good life and a favorable ultimate return.

The Surah reminds the Prophet that he has been sent to a community, as was the case with earlier messengers, to recite God’s revelation, even if some reject the Most Merciful. The Prophet’s role is to declare his reliance on God alone, who is the only true deity and the one to whom everyone will ultimately return.

Emphasizing the miraculous nature of the Qurʾān, it is stated that if any scripture could cause mountains to move, the earth to split, or the dead to speak, it would be this Qurʾān. But God alone determines all affairs, and if He had willed, everyone would have been guided. The disbelievers are warned that continuous calamities will befall them for their actions until God’s promise arrives, as God never breaks His word.

The Surah draws a historical parallel: previous messengers were mocked, but God gave their opponents time before ultimately punishing them. The implication is that the current rejection of Muḥammad fits a recurring pattern, and eventual divine retribution is inevitable.

The Surah questions the logic of associating partners with the all-knowing, all-maintaining God. The challenge is issued: if there are real partners to God, name them or show proof. In reality, such claims are based on delusion and self-deception. God allows those who persist in disbelief to go astray, and for them, there is no guide.
The punishment for such people begins in this life and will be far more severe in the Hereafter. They will have no protector against God’s judgment.
In contrast, the Surah describes Paradise as a place with rivers flowing beneath, unending fruit and shade — the reward for the righteous. The destiny of the disbelievers, by contrast, is the Fire.

The Surah notes that some among the People of the Book (Jews and Christians) rejoice at the Qurʾān, while others reject parts of it. The Prophet is instructed to clarify his mission: to worship God alone without associating partners, and to invite others to do the same, knowing that everyone will ultimately return to God.
The Qurʾān is described as an Arabic revelation containing laws and guidance. The Prophet is warned not to follow the desires of those who reject the message, as he would then lose God’s protection.

The Surah makes it clear that previous messengers were human beings who had families, and none could bring miracles except with God’s permission. Every matter is decreed at its appointed time, and God alone decides which parts of the revelation to confirm or abrogate, as He holds the “Mother of the Book” — the ultimate source of all scripture.

The Prophet’s mission is simply to deliver the message; whether he lives to see the fulfillment of God’s promises or not, his job is to warn, while God will hold people accountable. The Surah points to the ongoing loss of territory by those opposed to God’s message as a sign of divine judgment, stating that no one can overturn God’s decisions, and He brings events to account swiftly.

The Surah concludes by reminding that those before the current audience also made plans against God, but God’s plan supersedes all. He knows every soul’s actions, and in the end, the disbelievers will know who truly inherits the final home. The disbelievers challenge the Prophet’s legitimacy, but he is told to say that God and those who truly understand the scriptures are sufficient witnesses to his prophethood.

In summary, Sūrah ar-Raʿd lays out a comprehensive argument for the unity, power, and wisdom of God as demonstrated through the natural world, history, and revelation. It warns of the consequences of disbelief, urges personal responsibility and reform, and highlights the futility of worshipping other than God. The Surah uses parables, logical reasoning, and reminders of past peoples to call its audience to faith, patience, and obedience, assuring the righteous of Paradise and warning the heedless of divine retribution.

Sūrah Ibrāheem (Abraham) opens by declaring itself a divine revelation intended to lead humanity out of “darkness” (ignorance, misguidance) into “light” (knowledge, faith, guidance) with God’s permission. The path it calls to is that of Allah, described as all-powerful and worthy of praise. It establishes, right from the start, that all authority rests with Allah, who owns everything in the heavens and earth. A dire warning is issued to those who reject faith: they will face severe punishment, especially those who prioritize worldly life over the Hereafter, and who not only turn away from God’s way themselves but also actively mislead others.

The Surah emphasizes the universality and clarity of God’s message: every messenger is sent speaking the language of their people so that the message is unmistakable. Guidance and misguidance are ultimately in God’s hands, underscoring His sovereignty and wisdom. The narrative quickly shifts to history, specifically to the story of Mūsā (Moses) and his mission to bring the Israelites from darkness to light. Moses is told to remind his people of “the days of Allah”—moments when God’s intervention was clear, such as the deliverance from Firʿawn (Pharaoh), who brutally oppressed them, killing their sons and sparing their daughters. These were both trials and signs for those who are patient and grateful.

Central to the Surah is the theme of gratitude versus ingratitude. God’s fundamental promise is cited: if people are thankful, He increases them in blessings; if they are ungrateful, His punishment is severe. Moses cautions his people that disbelief affects only them, for God is infinitely self-sufficient. The Surah then invokes the fate of earlier nations—Nūḥ (Noah), ‘Ād, Thamūd, and others—who, despite receiving clear proofs from their messengers, stubbornly rejected faith and fell into doubt and denial.

The messengers’ dialogue with their people highlights key theological points: the reasonableness of believing in the Creator, the promise of forgiveness, and the reality of human mortality. Disbelievers, however, object that the messengers are merely men who seek to turn them from their ancestral ways and demand miraculous proof. The messengers respond that, though human, they are chosen by God and act only by His permission, placing their trust in Him and demonstrating patience in the face of hostility.

The hostility of those opposed to the message escalates to threats of exile or forced conversion. In response, God assures the messengers of eventual victory: the wrongdoers will be destroyed, and the faithful will inherit the land. This is conditional upon fearing God’s presence and warnings. The Surah records that the messengers prayed for God’s judgment, and ultimately, every arrogant tyrant is doomed to humiliation and punishment. The imagery here turns vivid: such tyrants are shown facing Hell, forced to drink foul, boiling water that they can barely swallow, assaulted by death from every side but never able to die, and tormented by even greater punishment.

The Surah then provides an analogy for the deeds of disbelievers: their actions are like ashes scattered by a fierce wind—utterly wasted and unrecoverable. This underscores the futility of actions not grounded in faith. God’s creative power is again highlighted: He brought the heavens and earth into existence and can easily replace humanity if He wills. On the Day of Judgment, everyone will be gathered before Him. Social hierarchies will dissolve; the weak followers will futilely seek help from their former leaders, who will admit their own helplessness and resignation to fate.

The Surah sets forth a powerful scene involving Shayṭān (Satan) after the final judgment. He confesses to humanity that, while God’s promise was true, his own promises were lies; he had no real power, only the ability to tempt, and people followed him of their own accord. Therefore, he disowns them and refuses any responsibility for their fate. This scene drives home the principle of personal accountability and the emptiness of excuses on the Day of Judgment. Those who did wrong will suffer severe punishment, while those who believed and did good will enter Jannah (Paradise), with rivers flowing beneath and greetings of “Peace!”

To reinforce these messages, the Surah uses parables. A “good word” (representing faith or truth) is likened to a “good tree” with deep roots and branches high in the sky, constantly bearing fruit by God’s permission. In contrast, a “bad word” (falsehood or disbelief) is like an uprooted, unstable tree. God keeps believers steadfast with this “firm word” in both this life and the next, while those who do wrong are led astray.

The Surah warns against those who squander God’s blessings by choosing disbelief, leading themselves and their people to ruin, which is identified as Hell. These people set up rivals to God and mislead others, but are told to enjoy their brief respite—ultimately, their destination is the Fire. The faithful, by contrast, are commanded to pray regularly and give charity, both openly and secretly, before a Day arrives when no ransom or friendship will save anyone.

The Surah then elaborates on God’s creative and providential power. He is the one who made the heavens, the earth, the rain, the fruits; He subjected the sea, the rivers, the sun, the moon, the night, and the day for humanity’s benefit. Not only has God provided for human needs, but He has given them even more than they have asked. Yet, the Surah laments, humans are typically unjust and ungrateful despite this overwhelming generosity.

The narrative then shifts to the figure of Ibrāheem (Abraham), whose prayer forms a central point in the Surah. Abraham prays for the security of Makkah, asking God to keep him and his descendants away from idol worship, acknowledging how many have been led astray by false gods. He expresses hope that those who follow him will be counted with him, but leaves the fate of the disobedient to God’s mercy and forgiveness.

Abraham recalls settling his family in a barren valley near the sacred Kaʿbah, praying that God will help them establish regular prayer, make people’s hearts kind toward them, and provide them with sustenance so they will be grateful. He acknowledges God’s omniscience—knowing all that is hidden and revealed—and praises Him for granting him sons, Ismāʿīl (Ishmael) and Isḥāq (Isaac), in old age. Abraham’s prayers continue, seeking that he and his descendants be devoted to prayer, and asking forgiveness for himself, his parents, and all believers on the Day of Judgment.

The Surah returns to the theme of divine justice. It assures that God is not unaware of what the wrongdoers do; rather, He is simply delaying their reckoning to a day so terrifying that people’s eyes will be transfixed, their hearts empty with fear. On that Day, the guilty will plead for more time, promising to follow God’s call and obey the messengers, but they will be reminded of their arrogant confidence and the lessons they ignored from the fate of earlier destroyed peoples.

The Surah points out that previous communities had planned against the messengers, but God’s plan ultimately prevails, no matter how formidable their efforts seem—even if their schemes could “move mountains.” The reliability of God’s promise to His messengers is then underlined: He will never fail them, for He is all-powerful and retributive.

The end of the world is described with apocalyptic imagery: the earth and heavens will be replaced with new ones, and all creatures will be summoned before God, the One who prevails over all. The guilty will be seen shackled together, wearing garments of pitch and their faces covered by flames. This horrific punishment is meant to ensure that every soul is repaid precisely for what it has earned, and a reminder that God’s reckoning is swift.

The Surah concludes by reaffirming its purpose: it is a declaration and warning to all people, so that they may realize there is only one God and that those who reflect and use their intellect will take heed. Sūrah Ibrāheem thus weaves together themes of monotheism, gratitude, prophetic history, divine justice, accountability, and the transience of worldly life, driving home the need for faith, right action, and preparation for the Hereafter.

Sūrah al-Ḥijr opens with a declaration that its verses are from the Book and a clear recitation—affirming the divine and lucid nature of the Qur’ān. It sets the stage by alluding to a future regret among those who disbelieve: one day, they will wish they had accepted Islam (submission to God). For now, these deniers are allowed to continue indulging in worldly pleasures and distractions, but the Surah warns that their ignorance and false hopes will eventually come to an end, and they will come to realize the truth.

The Surah then emphasizes the absolute control and decree of God (Allah) over the fate of nations and individuals.
