Every community that was destroyed met its end at a divinely appointed time—none could hasten or delay their destiny. This introduces a theme of divine justice and predetermined fate, underscoring that no nation or person can escape their allotted term, no matter their actions.

The attitude of the disbelievers toward Prophet Muhammad is described: they accuse him of madness and mock his message, demanding supernatural proof such as the visible descent of angels. The Surah replies that angels are only sent with truth and usually as a sign of the end—such a sign would leave them with no chance for repentance. Their demand is not sincere, but a manifestation of their stubborn disbelief.

A central reassurance is delivered: Allah Himself has sent down the Qur’ān and He will preserve it. This verse—famous in Islamic tradition—declares the divine protection of the Qur’ān from corruption or alteration, contrasting it with previous revelations whose followers failed to guard them.

The Surah reminds Muhammad that ridicule and rejection are not new; previous messengers faced the same treatment from their communities. This rejection is described as a condition placed in the hearts of those who transgress, who, despite evident signs, persist in denial. Even if they were to witness miraculous events, such as ascending through a gate in the sky, they would dismiss it as illusion or sorcery. Their disbelief is presented as willful and deep-seated, echoing the fate of earlier peoples who were destroyed for their obstinacy.

The Surah shifts to signs of God’s creative power in the universe. It describes the heavens adorned with stars, which are protected from devils who seek to eavesdrop on divine decrees. If such a devil attempts to steal a hearing, they are pursued by a burning flame. The earth is also highlighted: spread out, fortified with mountains, and containing a diversity of well-balanced plants. The Surah notes that Allah has provided livelihoods for humans and for creatures whom humans do not provide for—emphasizing the all-encompassing mercy and provision of God.

The discourse continues to stress Allah’s sovereignty and precise control: everything exists in measured quantities according to His knowledge and plan. Fertilizing winds, life-giving rain, and the very cycles of life and death are all under His command. Allah is described as the ultimate inheritor—everything returns to Him in the end. He is fully aware of all generations, past and future, and will gather all for accountability, acting with wisdom and knowledge.

The Surah then recounts the origins of humanity and the jinn. Humans were created from clay, specifically altered black mud, while the jinn were created earlier from scorching fire. This narrative introduces the story of Iblees (Satan), who refused God’s command to bow to Adam after God had fashioned and animated him. All the angels obeyed except Iblees, who was arrogant and refused to prostrate to a being made from clay.

Allah questions Iblees about his refusal, and Iblees responds with pride, claiming superiority over Adam due to his fiery origin. As a result, Allah expels Iblees from His presence and curses him until the Day of Judgment. Iblees requests a reprieve until the Resurrection, which Allah grants, but only for a specified time. Iblees then vows to mislead humanity, except for those who are sincerely devoted and chosen by God.

Allah asserts that Iblees will have no real authority over His true servants, but those who choose to follow Satan will be destined for Hell. The Surah vividly describes Hell as having seven gates, each assigned to a particular group of Satan’s followers—a powerful warning about the consequences of deviation.

By contrast, the Surah describes the fate of the righteous: they will be in gardens with flowing springs, greeted with peace and security. Any past resentment or ill-feeling will be removed from their hearts, so they will live as brothers, facing each other on thrones, completely free from fatigue or sorrow, and will never be expelled from this bliss.

The Surah then balances this with a reminder of Allah’s dual attributes: He is both supremely forgiving and merciful, yet also the possessor of a painful punishment. Both these aspects of divine reality must be communicated.

A major narrative section follows, recounting the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham) and the destruction of the people of Lūṭ (Lot). Angels visit Abraham, initially causing him fear, but they reassure him and give him the miraculous news of a son despite his old age. When Abraham expresses surprise, the angels confirm that nothing is impossible for God and that only the misguided despair of His mercy.

The angels then reveal that their primary mission is to punish a sinful people, except for the family of Lot, whom they will save—except for Lot’s wife, who is destined to remain behind. The story then shifts to Lot’s city, where the angels visit, and Lot’s people, notorious for their immoral behavior, approach with evil intent. Lot pleads with them to respect his guests and behave righteously, even offering his daughters in lawful marriage, but they are heedless, blinded by their passions.

The city is overtaken by a catastrophic punishment: a loud shriek and the overturning of the city, followed by a rain of stones. This destruction is presented as a lesson for those who think and a sign for the believers. The location of these destroyed towns on a well-known highway is emphasized, reinforcing that these are historical realities accessible to the audience’s knowledge.

The Surah briefly mentions the people of Madyan (the "companions of the thicket") and the people of al-Ḥijr (the Thamūd), both of whom denied their prophets and suffered divine retribution. The Thamūd, known for carving homes into mountains and feeling secure in their fortifications, were still destroyed by a sudden blast. Their material achievements could not save them—a warning against complacency and arrogance.

The Surah reaffirms that the universe was created with purpose and truth, not aimlessly. The coming of the Hour (the Day of Judgment) is a certainty, and the Prophet is told to forgive graciously, reflecting divine forbearance. God is described again as the all-knowing Creator.

Turning to Prophet Muhammad personally, the Surah reminds him of the special favor given to him: the seven oft-repeated verses (understood as Sūrah al-Fātiḥah) and the great Qur’ān. He is advised not to covet the worldly pleasures enjoyed by some disbelievers or feel sorrow for their fate. Instead, he is told to be gentle and kind to the believers and to focus on his role as a clear warner.

The Surah addresses opponents who divide Scripture into parts, accepting some and rejecting others, as previous communities had done. Such people will be held accountable for their actions and questioned by God about their conduct.

The Prophet is instructed to proclaim openly what he has been commanded, without fear, and to turn away from those who associate partners with God (the polytheists). God assures him of protection from those who mock and oppose him. Those who set up other deities alongside Allah will ultimately realize the error of their ways.

Recognizing the emotional burden placed on Muhammad by his people’s slander and opposition, the Surah offers spiritual medicine: he is told to glorify and praise God, to be among those who prostrate, and to continue worship until death—the ultimate certainty—arrives. This closes the Surah with a message of perseverance, devotion, and steadfastness in faith, regardless of opposition or hardship.

Sūrah an-Naḥl (“The Bee”) is a Meccan surah revealed during a period when the early Muslim community was facing increasing hostility and persecution. It is named after the mention of bees and their remarkable abilities as a sign of God’s wisdom. The surah provides a wide-ranging discourse that systematically addresses themes of divine signs in creation, the folly of idolatry, the certainty of resurrection, the duties of the Prophet, guidance for believers, warnings for disbelievers, and outlines of ethical and legal principles. Its tone alternates between rational argumentation, reminders of God’s favors, vivid eschatological warnings, and practical instructions for moral living.

The surah opens by declaring that God’s command and judgment are imminent, warning people not to be impatient for it. It sets the tone by affirming God’s transcendence above all forms of polytheism. God sends revelation through angels to chosen servants, commanding that people recognize His oneness and fear Him alone. The surah stresses repeatedly that God alone is the creator of the heavens and earth and everything within them, and that associating partners with Him is a grave error.

The surah then draws attention to various signs in nature and human life that indicate God’s creative power and mercy. It describes the creation of humanity from a mere sperm-drop, highlighting human frailty and the tendency to become argumentative and rebellious despite humble origins. Similarly, God’s creation of livestock is mentioned as a source of warmth, beauty, food, transport, and other benefits, all designed for human utility. Horses, mules, and donkeys are mentioned as further examples of God’s provision, as well as things beyond human knowledge yet to be discovered.

God’s guidance is emphasized as the true “right way,” while alternative paths lead astray. Rain, crops, fruit-bearing trees, and the cycles of day and night are all referenced as blessings and signs for those who reflect. The surah points to the sea, from which people derive food and ornaments, and the ships that traverse its vastness, all as evidence of divine favor and mastery. Mountains, rivers, roadways, and natural landmarks are mentioned as aids for human guidance and navigation, both physically and spiritually.

The surah then challenges idolatry by contrasting God, the Creator, with false gods who can create nothing and are themselves created, lifeless, and unaware of their followers’ actions. The surah asserts the oneness of God and notes that the hearts of those who deny the afterlife are arrogant and closed to the truth. God is fully aware of all that is concealed and revealed, and He does not love the arrogant.

The attitudes of the disbelievers are described: when asked about divine revelation, they dismiss it as myths. Such people will bear the consequences of their own sins and some of the sins of those they mislead. The surah recounts how previous peoples also plotted and built elaborate plans, but God’s punishment came upon them in unexpected ways, causing their schemes to collapse and their societies to be destroyed. On the Day of Resurrection, these deniers and wrongdoers will be publicly shamed and cast into Hell, while the righteous will receive a far better reward in the Hereafter.

The surah contrasts the fate of the arrogant wrongdoers with those who are mindful of God. The latter will declare that God’s revelation is good and beneficial, and they will be rewarded with eternal gardens where they can have whatever they desire. The angels will greet them with peace at death, affirming their entry into Paradise as a result of their deeds.

The surah notes that the only task of the messengers is to deliver God’s message clearly. It recounts how every nation received a prophet calling them to worship God alone and to avoid “ṭāghūt” (all forms of false gods and tyrannical forces). Some accepted guidance while others rejected it and suffered the consequences. The Prophet Muhammad is reassured that his efforts cannot guide everyone, for guidance and misguidance are ultimately in God’s hands.

A major theme is the reality of resurrection and the afterlife. The surah responds to those who deny bodily resurrection, stating that it is a true promise from God, easily fulfilled by His command. When God wills something, He simply says “Be,” and it is. The surah also acknowledges the sacrifices of those who emigrate for the cause of God, promising them good provision in this world and a greater reward in the Hereafter, provided they are patient and reliant on God.

The surah emphasizes the continuity of revelation, stating that previous prophets were all human beings chosen by God. It encourages those in doubt to consult knowledgeable people who possess earlier scriptures. God’s messengers brought clear signs and written ordinances. The Qur’an’s purpose is to clarify what people dispute, to provide guidance, and to encourage reflection.

The surah warns those who plot evil that God’s punishment can come suddenly, through natural disasters or gradual decline, and that none can escape His decree. All creation, even their shadows, submits to God in humility, and every creature in the heavens and on earth, including the angels, prostrates to Him. This universal submission is contrasted sharply with human arrogance and idolatry.

The surah stresses the futility of fearing or worshipping anything besides God, who alone controls the heavens and earth and deserves constant worship. Human beings tend to turn to God in times of distress but revert to polytheism or ingratitude when adversity is removed. The surah criticizes those who assign a share of their wealth or offerings to idols or to things they do not understand, and warns that they will be questioned about these false inventions.

The surah addresses the custom of attributing daughters to God while desiring sons for themselves, exposing the hypocrisy and injustice in such beliefs. It vividly describes the shame and distress with which some Arabs received news of a daughter’s birth, condemning female infanticide and the societal attitudes behind it. The surah asserts that such evil attitudes are only found among those who deny the Hereafter, while God is characterized by the highest and most perfect attributes.

God’s patience and mercy are highlighted: if He punished wrongdoing immediately, no creature would survive. Instead, He defers punishment to a fixed term. The surah criticizes the contradictory behavior of attributing what they themselves detest (daughters) to God, while expecting only good for themselves. Such people will face the Fire and be forsaken.

The surah recalls how past nations rejected their prophets, were deceived by Satan, and ultimately suffered painful consequences. The Qur’an is sent to clarify disputes, provide guidance, and serve as a mercy for believers.

Signs in nature are revisited: rain revives the earth, livestock provide milk—a pure, wholesome drink—while the fruits of date palms and grapevines are used both for sustenance and, in earlier times, for the production of intoxicants. The surah invites reflection on the bee, inspired by God to build hives and produce honey with healing properties, presenting this as a marvel of divine guidance.

The surah reminds people of their dependence on God throughout the stages of life, from ignorance at birth to senility in old age. Differences in wealth and provision are described as a test, and the folly of denying God’s favor is highlighted by noting that the privileged would not share their blessings equally with their slaves—so why do they deny God’s generosity?

The surah points to the blessings of family life: spouses, children, and grandchildren, all gifts from God, yet many respond with disbelief and ingratitude. The inability of idols to provide any benefit is contrasted with God’s continual provision from the heavens and earth.

Through parables, the surah illustrates the difference between God and idols: a helpless slave is not equal to a generous, free person, just as mute and useless individuals are not equal to those who command justice and follow a straight path. God alone possesses knowledge of the unseen, and the coming of the Hour (the Day of Judgment) is swift and certain.

The surah calls for gratitude, reminding humans that their faculties of hearing, sight, and intellect are divine gifts. It points to the marvel of birds in flight, homes and shelters, clothing for protection, and various forms of provision, urging recognition of God’s continuous favor.

The surah affirms that the Prophet’s duty is only to deliver the message clearly, even if people persist in denial. On the Day of Resurrection, every nation will have a witness against them (their prophet), and no excuses will be accepted from the disbelievers. Those who led others astray will be disavowed by their “partners” (idols), and all falsehoods will be exposed.

The surah declares that those who averted others from God’s path will receive compounded punishment. The Prophet is told that he will be a witness over his own community, and the Qur’an is described as clarification, guidance, mercy, and good news for those who submit to God (Muslims).

A concise set of ethical commands is then given: God enjoins justice, kindness, and generosity to relatives while forbidding immorality, wrongdoing, and tyranny. Believers are reminded to fulfill their covenants and oaths, not to use them deceitfully, and to remember that God is always aware of their actions.

The surah invokes the image of a woman who unravels her own hard-won spinning to illustrate the folly of breaking one’s solemn commitments for worldly gain or out of rivalry. People are tested in this way, and ultimate judgment is with God. The surah underscores that humanity could have been made a single religious community, but God’s wisdom allows for diversity and testing. All will be held accountable for their choices.

The surah warns against using oaths as a means of deception, as such behavior can lead to ruin and divine punishment, both in this world and the next. Believers are urged not to trade their covenant with God for fleeting worldly advantage, as God’s reward is lasting and far better.

The surah affirms that anyone—male or female—who does good deeds while believing will be granted a good life and a reward in the Hereafter based on the best of their actions. Before reciting the Qur’an, believers are advised to seek refuge in God from Satan, who has no real power over true believers but only over those who ally with him and commit idolatry.

The surah addresses accusations against the Prophet, such as the claim that he invented the Qur’an or learned it from a foreigner. It refutes these by noting the Qur’an’s clear Arabic language and the truthfulness of its message, brought by the angel Jibrīl (Gabriel) to strengthen the believers.

The surah makes a distinction between those who are compelled to outwardly deny faith (under duress) while their hearts remain firm in belief, and those who willingly choose disbelief. The former are excused, while the latter face God’s wrath and punishment because they prefer this worldly life over the Hereafter.

The surah provides a parable of a once-prosperous and secure city (interpreted as Makkah), which, after denying God’s favors and rejecting His messenger, experienced hunger and fear. This serves as a warning of the consequences of ingratitude.

The surah clarifies dietary laws, declaring certain things forbidden—such as carrion, blood, pork, and what is dedicated to other than God—but allowing exceptions in cases of necessity. It warns against inventing false religious prohibitions or claiming things are lawful or unlawful without divine sanction, as this is tantamount to fabricating lies about God.

The surah references the particular restrictions placed on the Jews as a result of previous transgressions, emphasizing that God did not wrong them; rather, they wronged themselves. Repentance and amending one’s ways are always open, and God remains forgiving and merciful.

The surah then presents Ibrāhīm (Abraham) as a model of faith: a leader, utterly devoted to God, grateful for His blessings, and free of all forms of idolatry. Abraham’s guidance and reward in both worlds is highlighted, and the Prophet Muhammad is instructed to follow the pure monotheistic path of Abraham. The specifics of the Sabbath are described as a matter for previous communities, and God alone will judge the disputes that arose over it.

The surah instructs the Prophet to invite others to God’s way using wisdom, gentle instruction, and the best manner of argumentation, recognizing that only God knows who is truly astray or rightly guided. It permits proportional retribution against enemies but strongly encourages patience and forgiveness as the better course.

Finally, the surah closes by reminding the Prophet that patience is only possible through God’s help and that he should not grieve over those who refuse to believe or plot against him. God is always with those who are conscious of Him and do good. Throughout the surah, there is a persistent call to recognize the signs of God in creation, heed His guidance, live ethically, and prepare for inevitable accountability in the Hereafter.

Sūrah al-Isrā’ (The Night Journey), also known as Sūrah Banī Isrā’īl, opens with a reference to one of the most significant events in the life of Prophet Muḥammad: the Isra, or night journey. It declares that God is supremely exalted, having taken His servant Muḥammad by night from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām (the Sacred Mosque in Mecca) to al-Masjid al-Aqṣā (the Farthest Mosque, generally understood as Jerusalem), a journey filled with divine signs. This verse sets the tone for the Surah, which is concerned with the miraculous, the responsibilities of faith, and the consequences of obedience and disobedience.

The Surah then transitions into a historical reflection on previous communities, notably the Children of Israel. It recalls that Mūsā (Moses) was given scripture as guidance, with an explicit command that they should depend solely on God as their protector. The narrative reminds the Children of Israel that they are the descendants of those saved with Nūḥ (Noah) and highlights the importance of gratitude, as exemplified by Noah. The Surah foretells that the Children of Israel would twice cause corruption and become arrogant on earth, leading to punishment at the hands of powerful enemies who would devastate their land, including their temple in Jerusalem. However, after the first punishment, they would experience a resurgence, regaining strength and numbers, but if they persisted in wrongdoing, another destruction would follow. Still, the door to repentance and divine mercy remains open, with the warning that continued rejection would result in Hell as a final abode for the disbelievers.

The Surah asserts the Qur’an’s universal guidance, promising a great reward for believers who perform righteous deeds, while warning of painful punishment for those who reject the Hereafter. It observes the impulsiveness of human nature—people hastily pray for both good and bad things, not realizing the weight of their requests. The alternation of night and day is described as deliberate, with each serving as a sign; day’s clarity is for seeking livelihood and marking time, emphasizing God’s intricate management of creation.

Individual accountability is a central theme: every person’s destiny is metaphorically fastened to their own neck, and on the Day of Resurrection, each will be presented with a comprehensive record of their deeds—no one will bear the burden of another. Divine justice requires that God only punishes a community after sending it a messenger. When a society’s affluent are commanded and persist in defiance, total destruction follows, as happened to many past generations after Noah. This serves as a warning, highlighting God’s awareness of people’s actions and the inevitability of consequences.

The Surah contrasts those who chase immediate worldly gains with those who sincerely strive for the Hereafter. Those fixated on this life may get some of its rewards but will ultimately face humiliation and Hell, while those seeking the Hereafter with faith and effort will have their endeavors appreciated. Divine generosity is not limited; both groups receive from God’s bounty in this world, but the Hereafter will reveal far greater distinctions. The Surah warns against associating others with God, reiterating the principle of pure monotheism.

A series of ethical injunctions follow, forming a foundational moral code. First and foremost is the exclusive worship of God. Special emphasis is placed on kind and respectful treatment of parents, particularly in their old age, with instructions to avoid even minor expressions of annoyance and to pray for their well-being. God knows the intentions behind people’s actions and is forgiving to the sincerely penitent.

Social responsibilities are detailed: relatives, the poor, and travelers have a right to assistance, but this is not a license for wastefulness. Wastefulness is likened to the behavior of devils, who are ungrateful to God. If one lacks the means to help, they are advised to speak kindly rather than harshly. The Surah advocates a balanced approach to spending—neither miserly nor reckless—to avoid blame and poverty, recognizing that God alone controls provision.

The sanctity of life is affirmed; children must not be killed out of fear of poverty, as God provides for all. Unlawful sexual relations are strictly prohibited as immoral and destructive. Murder is forbidden except in the course of justice, with provisions for legal retribution but strict warnings against excess or vigilantism. The property of orphans is to be protected and only managed for their benefit until maturity. Fulfilling one’s commitments is stressed as a matter of accountability before God.

Honesty in trade is mandated: fair measure and weight are required, as is refraining from pursuing matters about which one has no knowledge. The faculties of hearing, sight, and intellect will all be subject to questioning. Arrogance is denounced; people are reminded of their limitations—they cannot break the earth or rival the mountains. All such evil behaviors are detested by God.

The Surah returns to theological themes, warning against associating partners with God and exposing the irrationality of claims about God having sons or angels as daughters. The Qur’an’s varied presentations are reminders, yet they only increase aversion among some disbelievers. The impossibility of rival deities is underscored—if there were other gods, they would attempt to usurp God’s throne, but God is exalted beyond such claims.

The Surah further describes how all of creation—heavens, earth, and everything within—glorify God, even if humans fail to perceive this. When the Qur’an is recited, a spiritual barrier is placed between believers and those who deny the afterlife, preventing the latter from understanding it. Their spiritual blindness and aversion are attributed to their own stubbornness, not a lack of evidence.

The disbelievers’ response to the Prophet is characterized by ridicule and demands for miraculous signs or physical manifestations of resurrection. The Surah answers their skepticism by asserting that God, who created everything in the first place, can easily resurrect people. The Day will come when everyone will be called and judged, with each person’s own record serving as witness.

The Surah addresses the Prophet directly, reminding him that guidance and misguidance are in God’s hands. He is not responsible for people’s choices but is simply a messenger. The Surah also affirms the hierarchy among prophets—God has favored some above others, with Dāwūd (David) receiving the Psalms.

The futility of calling upon other beings besides God is exposed; even those invoked as deities strive themselves to be nearer to God, fearing His punishment and hoping for His mercy. No city will escape God’s judgment—either destruction or severe punishment will reach every community before the Day of Resurrection, as decreed in God’s register.

The Surah explains why God does not overwhelm people with overt miracles—past peoples denied such signs, like the people of Thamūd who rejected the she-camel. Miracles serve as warnings, and their rejection only deepens people’s defiance. The Prophet is reminded that the visions shown to him (possibly referring to the Night Journey or a vision of future events) are also a test for people and that some (like the cursed tree of Zaqqūm) serve as warnings that only increase some in rebelliousness.

The Surah retells the story of Iblīs (Satan) refusing to bow to Adam out of pride, declaring his intention to mislead Adam’s descendants. God permits Satan to attempt to lead astray those who choose to follow, promising that Hell will be the recompense for both him and his followers. Satan is given free rein to tempt humans through various means, but he has no real authority over the sincere servants of God, for God alone is the ultimate Protector.

The Surah then reflects on human behavior in the face of adversity and blessing. At sea, when in danger, people call solely upon God, but when saved, they quickly forget Him. The Surah warns against feeling secure from God’s power—He can cause calamities on land or sea at any time, and no one can intercede or avenge against Him.

Human beings—children of Adam—are reminded of the honor given them by God: they are carried across land and sea, provided with good things, and favored over much of creation. Yet, ultimate accountability lies ahead, when every community will be summoned with its record, and each person will be judged with perfect justice.

Spiritual blindness is emphasized: those who are blind to the truth in this world will remain blind in the Hereafter, more astray than ever. The Surah recounts the pressure placed on the Prophet to compromise the revelation in exchange for acceptance and the divine support that kept him firm. Had he yielded, he would have faced severe consequences, both in this life and the next.

The Surah touches on the attempts by the disbelievers of Mecca to expel the Prophet from the city, warning that their own destruction would swiftly follow such an act, as happened with previous nations who rejected their prophets.

Ritual and spiritual discipline are addressed: the Surah commands the establishment of prayer at specific times—from the decline of the sun until night and especially at dawn, which is witnessed by angels. It encourages extra prayer in the night (tahajjud) for the Prophet, with the hope that God will raise him to a "praised station" in the Hereafter.

The Prophet is instructed to pray for honorable entry and exit (possibly relating to migration and other transitions) and to seek support from God. The Surah proclaims the arrival of truth and the inevitable disappearance of falsehood. The Qur’an is described as a source of healing and mercy for believers, while for wrongdoers, it only increases their loss.

Human nature is again examined: when blessed, people tend to turn away from God, but when hardship strikes, they fall into despair. Each person acts according to their own character, but God knows best who is rightly guided.

The Surah addresses a question about the soul (rūḥ), stating that knowledge of its reality is limited and belongs solely to God, demonstrating the boundaries of human knowledge. It affirms the divine protection over the Qur’an—if God willed, He could remove it, but its preservation is a mercy.

The inimitability of the Qur’an is asserted: neither humans nor jinn could ever produce anything like it, even if they collaborated. The Qur’an contains every conceivable example and lesson, but most people persist in disbelief. The disbelievers make impossible demands for miracles and physical proofs, but the Prophet is reminded that he is only a human messenger.

The Surah responds to the objection that a human messenger cannot be sent by God, arguing that if angels lived on earth, an angel would have been sent. God is sufficient as witness over the truth of the Prophet’s mission. Guidance and misguidance are entirely in God’s hands; those led astray will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in utter humiliation, being blind, mute, and deaf, condemned to Hell for their denial and skepticism regarding resurrection.

The Surah revisits the story of Moses and Pharaoh, recalling the nine miraculous signs given to Moses, Pharaoh’s accusation of sorcery, and the eventual destruction of Pharaoh and his followers. After their deliverance, the Children of Israel are told to settle in the land, with the promise that they will be gathered together again at the final hour.

The Surah concludes by affirming that the Qur’an was revealed in truth and that the Prophet’s mission is to deliver good news and warnings. The gradual revelation of the Qur’an is highlighted as a means for the Prophet to recite it to the people over time. Those who were given prior knowledge (from previous scriptures) recognize its truth and respond with humility and worship, while others persist in disbelief.

Instructions are given about calling upon God by His various beautiful names, with guidance to pray neither too loudly nor too softly but in moderation. The Surah ends with a declaration of God’s absolute uniqueness: He has no offspring, no partners, and no need for protection. The Prophet is directed to continually praise and glorify God, reaffirming His transcendence and sovereignty.

Sūrah al-Kahf (“The Cave”), a chapter revealed in the middle Makkan period when the early Muslim community faced mounting opposition, opens with praise for God (Allāh) as the One who sent the Qur’an to His servant, Muḥammad, making it a book with no deviation or error. The surah immediately establishes the Qur’an’s purpose: to serve as a clear, unerring warning of severe punishment for those who reject faith, and as glad tidings for those who believe and perform good deeds that they will have an everlasting, excellent reward in Paradise (Jannah). The surah also specifically warns against attributing a son to God, criticizing those who make such claims as uttering lies without knowledge and reminding them of the gravity of such statements. The Prophet is addressed directly, expressing God’s awareness of his deep sorrow and anguish over the disbelief of others, but reminding him that guidance is ultimately in God’s hands.

The surah sets out the centrality of this world as a test, describing all that is on earth as a temporary adornment, designed to distinguish those whose actions are best. But ultimately, all of earth’s beauty will be reduced to barren dust, emphasizing the fleeting nature of material life. This theme of testing and the impermanence of worldly attractions recurs throughout the surah.

The first major narrative is the story of the Companions of the Cave (Aṣḥāb al-Kahf), a group of God-fearing youths who, facing persecution for their monotheistic faith, withdrew from their idolatrous society and sought refuge in a cave, praying for God’s mercy and guidance. God responded by causing them to sleep in the cave for many years, protecting them from their enemies. When they eventually awoke, the passage of time became clear through their own confusion and the subsequent discovery by townspeople, serving as a sign of God’s power over life, death, and resurrection, and as evidence for the reality of the coming Hour (the Day of Judgment).

The surah delves into various details of this story: the firmness of the youths’ faith, their reasoning in rejecting idolatry, and their reliance on God’s mercy. It describes miraculous aspects of their sleep—the sun’s movement sparing them, their turning in sleep, and their dog stationed at the cave’s entrance. Their awakening leads to a cautious attempt to re-enter society, only to be discovered, catalyzing debates among the people about the number of the sleepers and their significance. The surah cautions against fruitless speculation about their details and stresses that only God truly knows such matters. Through this story, the surah underlines the importance of saying “If God wills” (in shā’ Allāh) when speaking about future intentions, highlighting human limitation and dependence on divine will.

The narrative of the Companions of the Cave closes by restating God’s exclusive knowledge of the unseen and His sole authority over creation and legislation. The Prophet is instructed to recite what has been revealed, reminding all that God’s words are unchangeable and that there is no refuge except with Him.

Moving from narrative to practical instruction, the surah urges the Prophet to remain patient and steadfast with sincere believers—those who faithfully engage in worship morning and evening—rather than seeking the company or approval of the wealthy or heedless. It warns against being distracted by worldly allurements and cautions not to obey those whose hearts are neglectful of God’s remembrance and who follow their base desires. The surah then lays out a principle of individual responsibility: “The truth is from your Lord. Whoever wills, let him believe; whoever wills, let him disbelieve.” However, it follows with a stark warning of Hellfire for wrongdoers, describing its horror in vivid terms, and a contrasting promise of unending reward, luxury, and comfort in Paradise for those who believe and do good.

The surah presents the parable of two men, one of whom is granted two flourishing gardens and abundant wealth. This man boasts of his superiority and falls into arrogance, doubting the reality of the Hereafter and assuming his wealth makes him secure. His companion, though less wealthy, reminds him of God’s power and the transience of worldly blessings, urging humility and gratitude. The narrative culminates when the arrogant man’s gardens are destroyed suddenly, leaving him in regret and despair, recognizing too late the folly of associating anyone with God or relying on material possessions. This story exemplifies the dangers of pride, the fragility of worldly wealth, and the virtue of trust in and thankfulness to God.

To reinforce the message, the surah provides another parable: the life of this world is likened to rain that brings forth lush vegetation, which quickly withers and is blown away by the wind, illustrating the fleeting nature of worldly achievements and beauty. It asserts that while wealth and children are adornments of this temporary life, “lasting good deeds” are far better in God’s estimation, both as a reward and as a source of hope.

Shifting to eschatology, the surah vividly depicts scenes from the Day of Judgment: the mountains will be removed, the earth laid bare, and all people gathered before God, unable to hide anything. Their deeds will be presented in a complete record, and the guilty will be terrified by its accuracy, realizing that nothing has been omitted. Justice will be absolute and no one will be wronged. The surah then reminds listeners of the primordial story of Adam and Iblīs (Satan): when God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, all obeyed except Iblīs, who was of the jinn and rebelled. The surah warns against taking Satan and his progeny as allies, given their enmity to humanity.

The surah continues with theological clarifications: God did not require help from anyone in creating the heavens, the earth, or humanity, nor does He need misguided beings as assistants. On the Day of Judgment, those who worshipped false deities will find them powerless to help, and the criminals will be confronted with Hell, certain of their fate with no escape.

The surah draws attention to the fact that the Qur’an contains a wide variety of lessons, parables, and warnings, but many people persist in argument and disbelief. It laments that the only thing preventing people from embracing guidance and seeking forgiveness is their attachment to the ways of previous destroyed nations, or their demand that punishment befall them immediately. The function of messengers is restated: to convey good news and warnings, but the disbelievers mock and dispute, turning God’s signs and the warnings into objects of ridicule. Those who refuse to heed reminders are described as having their hearts and ears sealed, rendering them incapable of receiving guidance. Nevertheless, God’s forgiveness and mercy are emphasized—He does not rush to punish, but gives people time and opportunity.
The surah gives a brief historical reflection: previous communities that persisted in wrongdoing were destroyed at their appointed time, underscoring the certainty and justice of divine retribution.

The next major narrative is the story of Mūsā (Moses) and al-Khiḍr. Moses, seeking deeper knowledge, embarks on a journey with his companion (traditionally identified as his servant, Yūshaʿ/Joshua) to the junction of the two seas. Along the way, a forgotten fish serves as a sign, leading them to al-Khiḍr, a mysterious servant to whom God has given unique knowledge and mercy. Moses asks to accompany al-Khiḍr to learn from him, but is warned that he will not be able to patiently endure actions whose wisdom he cannot comprehend. Moses agrees to refrain from questioning, but soon struggles to keep his promise.

Together, they encounter three incidents: first, al-Khiḍr deliberately damages a ship belonging to poor people, prompting Moses’ protest; second, al-Khiḍr kills a seemingly innocent boy, again shocking Moses; third, after being refused hospitality in a town, al-Khiḍr repairs a collapsing wall for free, leading Moses to suggest he should have been paid. At each step, Moses questions or comments, and al-Khiḍr reminds him of the prior agreement. Finally, al-Khiḍr explains the hidden wisdom behind each act: the ship was damaged to save it from being seized by a tyrant king; the boy, if left alive, would have grown to become a source of grief and disbelief for his believing parents, so God intended to replace him with a better child; the wall concealed a treasure belonging to two orphans, and repairing it ensured they would inherit it when mature, as a mercy due to their righteous father. Al-Khiḍr makes clear he acted by God’s instruction, not personal whim, demonstrating that divine wisdom often lies beyond human perception.

The surah then addresses a question often raised to the Prophet about Dhul-Qarnayn (“the Two-Horned One”), a powerful and just ruler. God establishes that He granted Dhul-Qarnayn authority and means to accomplish great things. The narrative describes his journeys to the far west and east, where he interacts with various peoples, dispensing justice: punishing wrongdoers and rewarding the righteous. On another journey, he encounters a people threatened by the destructive tribes of Gog and Magog (Ya’jūj and Ma’jūj). Refusing payment, Dhul-Qarnayn, with their help, constructs a massive barrier of iron and molten copper to contain the threat. He attributes this achievement to God’s mercy and warns that when God’s appointed time arrives, the barrier will collapse, allowing Gog and Magog to surge forth—a reference to apocalyptic events preceding the Day of Judgment.

The surah returns to eschatological themes, describing chaos and accountability on the Last Day: people will be gathered in throngs, Hell will be presented to the disbelievers, and those who neglected God’s remembrance will face the consequences. It criticizes those who seek aid from anyone but God, reiterating that Hell is prepared for them. A poignant section follows, identifying the “greatest losers” as those whose lives are wasted in pursuit of worldly deeds that ultimately amount to nothing because of their disbelief and mockery of God’s signs and messengers. In contrast, those who believe and act righteously are promised the highest gardens of Paradise, where they will dwell eternally, never wishing for any change.

The surah concludes by affirming God’s infinite knowledge and power, stating that even if the sea were ink, it would be exhausted before God’s words and wisdom were exhausted. The Prophet is reminded to declare his humanity and his sole distinction: receiving revelation that God is One. The final instruction is a succinct summary of Islamic religious ethos: anyone who hopes to meet God should do righteous deeds and avoid associating any partners with Him in worship.

Throughout Sūrah al-Kahf, the repeated motifs are clear: God’s absolute oneness and authority, the fleeting nature of worldly life, the certainty of resurrection and judgment, the importance of humble faith and righteous action, the dangers of arrogance, and the limits of human knowledge compared to God’s wisdom. The surah employs powerful stories, parables, and warnings to guide, instruct, and caution, offering both comfort and admonition to those who reflect.

Sūrah Maryam ("Mary") opens with a sequence of Arabic letters (Kāf, Hā, Yā, 'Ayn, Ṣād), which are enigmatic and found at the beginnings of several chapters in the Quran. The Surah is named after Maryam (Mary), the mother of ʿĪsā (Jesus), and was revealed in the early Makkan period when Muslims faced increasing opposition. The Surah focuses on stories of several prophets, emphasizing divine mercy, the miraculous nature of God's power, and the importance of sincere faith.

The Surah begins by recounting the story of Zakariyyā (Zechariah), a prophet who, in his old age and with a barren wife, prays privately and earnestly to God for a righteous heir. Zechariah expresses his frailty and concern for his legacy, desiring a child who would inherit not only his material possessions but, more importantly, his spiritual mission and the legacy of the family of Yaʿqūb (Jacob). God responds to his prayer, announcing the forthcoming birth of Yaḥyā (John), a name not previously given to anyone, signifying the uniqueness of this child.

Zechariah, astonished due to his and his wife's advanced age, questions how this could be possible. The angel assures him that for God, creating life is effortless, reminding Zechariah of his own creation from nothing. Zechariah requests a sign, and God grants it: he will be unable to speak to people for three nights while remaining otherwise healthy. Zechariah then emerges from his sanctuary, using gestures to instruct his people to glorify God morning and evening.

The narrative shifts to Yaḥyā (John), who is commanded by God to hold firmly to the divine scripture. Even as a child, John is granted wisdom, compassion, and purity, and he is noted for his deep reverence for God, his kindness to his parents, and his avoidance of arrogance or rebellion. The Surah invokes peace upon John at his birth, his death, and his resurrection, underscoring his blessed status at every stage of existence.

The Surah then turns to the story of Maryam (Mary), who withdraws from her family to a secluded eastern place. During her solitude, the angel Jibrīl (Gabriel) appears to her as a man. Alarmed, Mary seeks protection in God but is reassured by the angel, who informs her that she will miraculously bear a "pure boy" (Jesus). Mary questions how this can be, given her chastity. The angel responds that God's will makes all things possible, and that her son will be a sign for humanity and a manifestation of divine mercy. The conception occurs without human intervention, and Mary retreats to a remote place, burdened by the pains of childbirth and despairing to the point of wishing for death.

In her moment of despair, a voice (interpreted as either Jesus or an angel) comforts her, telling her not to grieve and pointing out a stream provided by God. She is instructed to shake the trunk of a palm tree, causing fresh dates to fall for her sustenance. Mary is further advised that if she encounters anyone, she should indicate she has vowed silence to the Most Merciful. When Mary returns to her community carrying the infant Jesus, they are shocked and accuse her of immorality, referencing her pious ancestry.

In response, Mary simply points to her infant son. The people are incredulous, questioning how a baby could speak. Jesus then miraculously speaks from the cradle, declaring himself a servant of God, a recipient of revelation, and a prophet. He proclaims that God has made him blessed, enjoined him to prayer and charity, and commanded him to be dutiful to his mother, not arrogant or rebellious. Jesus invokes peace upon himself at birth, death, and resurrection, paralleling the earlier blessing upon John.

The Surah clarifies that this is the true account of Jesus, son of Mary, about which people dispute. It emphatically denies the idea that God has a son, declaring that God simply wills things into being by saying "Be," and they are. Jesus himself is quoted as calling for exclusive worship of God, identifying this as the straight path. Despite this clear message, divisions and confusion arose among later communities regarding Jesus’ nature. The Surah warns of dire consequences for those who reject the truth, especially on the "Day of Regret" when ultimate realities are revealed, and stresses God's sovereignty over all creation.

The narrative continues with the story of Ibrāhīm (Abraham), recognized for his truthfulness and prophethood. The Surah recounts Abraham's gentle, reasoned appeals to his father, urging him to abandon idol worship for the worship of the one true God, and warning of the consequences of following Satan. Abraham’s father rejects his son’s advice and threatens him with violence, at which point Abraham promises to pray for his father’s forgiveness and peacefully distances himself from his family’s practices. As a reward for his faith, God grants Abraham sons (Isḥāq/Isaac and Yaʿqūb/Jacob), both made prophets, and bestows upon their lineage mercy and honor.

The Surah then highlights other prophets: Mūsā (Moses), chosen by God as messenger and prophet, who was spoken to directly by God on the side of Mount Sinai and given his brother Hārūn (Aaron) as a prophet; Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), praised for his truthfulness, faithfulness to promises, and dedication to prayer and charity; and Idrīs (Enoch), who is described as trustworthy and elevated to a high status. These accounts serve to demonstrate God’s favor upon the righteous among Adam’s descendants, Noah’s followers, Abraham’s family, and the children of Israel.

The Surah contrasts these exemplary figures with later generations who neglected prayer and followed their own desires. It warns that such conduct leads to severe punishment, but simultaneously offers hope: those who repent, believe, and act righteously are promised entry into Jannah (Paradise) without injustice. Paradise is described as a place of perpetual gardens, peace, and uninterrupted provision, fulfilling the unseen promise of God to His devoted servants.

At this point, the Surah addresses the nature and role of the angels, particularly Jibrīl, who clarifies that angels only descend by God’s command. Everything in existence—past, present, and future—belongs to God, who is never forgetful. God is described as the Lord of the heavens and the earth and everything in between, unmatched by any other being. The Surah urges patience and steadfastness in worship, reminding humans of their dependence on God and the futility of denying resurrection.

The Surah challenges the skepticism of those who doubt resurrection after death, reminding them that God created humans from nothing in the first place. It asserts that God will inevitably gather all people and the devils on the Day of Judgment, bringing them to Hell in a state of humiliation. From every group, the most defiant will be singled out for punishment, and God alone knows who deserves the fire. Every person will encounter Hell, but God will rescue the righteous while abandoning the wrongdoers within it.

The Surah also addresses the pride and arrogance of disbelievers who mock the believers’ social standing and material possessions, claiming superiority. God rebuts this by recalling past generations who were far wealthier and more impressive yet were destroyed for their arrogance. The Surah explains that the apparent extension of time or increase in worldly goods for wrongdoers is merely a reprieve before their eventual reckoning. True superiority lies in enduring good deeds, which carry the greatest reward and ultimate return in God’s estimation.

The Surah refutes the baseless claims of disbelievers who assert they will be given wealth and children in the afterlife. God questions whether such claims are based on knowledge of the unseen or a divine guarantee. Instead, God warns that He will record their statements and increase their punishment. On the Day of Judgment, everyone will stand alone before God, stripped of all false claims and earthly attachments.

The Surah further denounces the worship of false deities, explaining that these so-called gods will disavow their worshippers and even become adversaries to them on Judgment Day. The Surah highlights the role of devils in inciting disbelief and evil, but reassures the Prophet not to be impatient for the punishment of the disbelievers, as their time is strictly limited by God.

On the Day of Judgment, God will honor the righteous, bringing them as a welcomed delegation, while the guilty will be driven to Hell in thirst and humiliation. No one will be able to intercede for another except those who have a special covenant with God. The Surah strongly condemns the assertion that God has a son, describing this as a monstrous claim so grave that it threatens the very fabric of the cosmos. Every creature, the Surah insists, comes before God as a servant, individually accounted for and alone on the Day of Resurrection.

The Surah concludes with a note of comfort and encouragement for the Prophet Muḥammad, stating that the Quran has been made easy in Arabic so he can give glad tidings to the righteous and warn those who are hostile. The Surah ends by reminding that many generations before have been destroyed for their arrogance, leaving no trace behind—a sobering reminder of the fleeting nature of worldly power and the enduring truth of God’s message.

Sūrah Ṭā Hā begins by emphasizing that the Qur’an was not sent to burden or distress the Prophet Muḥammad, but rather as a reminder and guidance for those who are mindful of God. The opening lines remind the reader that this revelation comes from the One who created the earth and the highest heavens, and who is supremely merciful and sovereign over all creation. God’s knowledge encompasses everything, including what is spoken openly and what is kept even more hidden, affirming His absolute authority and the uniqueness of His divinity.

The Surah then turns to the story of Mūsā (Moses), one of the most important prophets in Islamic tradition, introducing it as a narrative of great significance. It recounts the moment when Moses, while traveling with his family, sees a fire and approaches it, hoping for guidance or a torch. At the fire, God calls to Moses, instructing him to remove his sandals, for he is in the sacred valley of Ṭuwā, and reveals to him his prophetic mission. God declares His oneness and commands Moses to worship Him and establish prayer as a means of remembrance. Moses is told about the coming of the Hour (the Day of Judgment), which God nearly conceals so that every soul may be recompensed for its actions, and is warned not to let deniers distract him from this reality.

God then engages Moses in a dialogue about the staff in his hand, which Moses uses in his daily life. God instructs him to cast it down, whereupon it becomes a living snake. God reassures Moses, telling him not to fear, and returns the staff to its original form. Moses is also given the sign of his hand, which, when drawn out, turns white without disease. These signs are presented as evidence of God’s power, meant to strengthen Moses for his mission to confront Firʿawn (Pharaoh), who has become a tyrant.

Before embarking on his mission, Moses prays for God to expand his heart, ease his task, untie the knot from his tongue so he can speak clearly, and appoint his brother Hārūn (Aaron) as his assistant. God grants these requests, reminding Moses of earlier favors: his miraculous survival as an infant, when his mother placed him in a chest in the river to escape Pharaoh’s edict, his return to his mother, his upbringing under God’s watchful care, his escape from Egypt after unintentionally killing a man, and his years in Madyan. All these events, God says, were part of preparing Moses for his prophetic role.

God instructs both Moses and Aaron to go to Pharaoh with His signs and to speak gently to him, in hopes that Pharaoh may remember or fear God. Moses and Aaron express fear that Pharaoh will punish or exceed all bounds with them, but God reassures them of His presence, protection, and knowledge. They are told to demand that Pharaoh release the Banī Isrā’īl (Children of Israel) and not torment them, warning that punishment awaits those who deny and turn away from God’s guidance.

The confrontation with Pharaoh is recounted in detail. Pharaoh questions Moses about his Lord, to which Moses replies that their Lord is the One who shaped all things and guides them. Pharaoh presses him about the fate of previous generations, and Moses replies that their knowledge is with God, who neither errs nor forgets. Moses describes God’s blessings—providing the earth, pathways, rain, and plant life, and reminds Pharaoh of human origins, mortality, and resurrection.

Despite being shown all these signs, Pharaoh rejects them and accuses Moses of sorcery, proposing a contest between Moses and Pharaoh’s magicians. A public appointment is set for the confrontation. When the day comes, the magicians cast their ropes and staffs, which appear to move like snakes due to their magic, causing Moses anxiety. God reassures Moses, instructing him to throw his staff, which miraculously devours the magicians’ tricks. Realizing the truth, the magicians fall in prostration, declaring belief in the Lord of Moses and Aaron.

Pharaoh, furious, accuses the magicians of conspiring with Moses and threatens them with severe punishment—amputation and crucifixion. The magicians, undeterred, affirm their faith in God, preferring divine forgiveness and truth over Pharaoh’s threats, and acknowledging that Pharaoh’s authority is only over this worldly life. They contrast the ultimate fate of those who come to God as criminals—eternal torment in Hell, neither dying nor truly living—with the reward of believers who purify themselves: eternal gardens with rivers flowing beneath.

The narrative continues with the exodus. God inspires Moses to lead the Israelites out of Egypt by night and strike a dry path through the sea, promising safety from Pharaoh. Pharaoh and his armies pursue and are drowned, while the Israelites are delivered. Pharaoh’s misguidance of his people is noted. God reminds the Israelites of His favor in saving them, making an appointment with them at Mount Sinai, and providing them with manna and quails, but also warns them not to abuse these blessings or be ungrateful, lest God’s anger descend upon them. Yet, God affirms that He is always ready to forgive those who repent, believe, do righteous deeds, and remain steadfast in guidance.

The Surah addresses the episode of the golden calf. As Moses hastens to meet God, God informs him that his people have been tested in his absence and led astray by the Sāmirī (the Samaritan). Upon his return, Moses is angered and saddened to find that the people have made a calf statue from their jewelry, claiming it is their god. Aaron had tried to warn them and urge them to remain faithful to God, but most refused to listen. Moses reproaches Aaron for not preventing their deviation, but Aaron explains that he feared causing division.

Moses then confronts the Sāmirī, who confesses that he took a handful from the track of the messenger (interpreted by commentators as either Gabriel or a divine sign) and was enticed by his own soul to create the calf. Moses condemns him to isolation (“No contact”) and warns of a future reckoning. The golden calf is burned and its ashes cast into the sea, emphasizing the futility of idolatry. The Surah reiterates that the only true god is God, who encompasses all knowledge.

Returning to the present, the Surah addresses the Prophet Muḥammad, reminding him that such stories are recounted as part of the divine message given to him. Those who turn away from God’s message will face a great burden on the Day of Resurrection, carrying their sins eternally, a terrible fate.

The Surah vividly describes scenes from the Day of Judgment: the blowing of the Horn, criminals gathered with blue eyes (a sign of fear or disgrace), people arguing over how long they stayed in the world—ten days, one day, or only a little—showing their confusion and regret. The mountains will be leveled, the earth flattened, and all will be summoned by a single caller with no escape. Voices will fall silent before the Most Merciful, and only those granted permission by God will be able to intercede.

God’s perfect knowledge, encompassing all past and future, is highlighted, while humans cannot grasp the full scope of His wisdom. On that Day, all faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer, and those who carry injustice will fail. In contrast, those who do good while believing will not fear injustice or loss.

The Surah reaffirms the purpose and method of revelation: the Qur’an is sent in clear Arabic, with varied warnings and reminders, so that people might avoid sin or at least recall the truth. The Prophet is cautioned not to rush in reciting the revelation before it is completed, and is encouraged to seek increase in knowledge through prayer.

Another major narrative follows: the story of Ādam (Adam). God recalls how He took a covenant with Adam, but Adam forgot and lacked firm resolve. The angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, but Iblīs (Satan) refused. God warns Adam and his wife that Satan is their enemy and not to let him drive them from Jannah (Paradise), where they would live in comfort, free from hunger, thirst, or heat.

Despite the warning, Satan deceives Adam into thinking that eating from the forbidden tree would grant eternal life or lasting dominion. When Adam and his wife eat from it, their nakedness becomes apparent, and they cover themselves with leaves. Adam’s disobedience is acknowledged, but God chooses him again, forgives him, and guides him.

God then commands Adam and his progeny to descend from Paradise, warning that enmity will exist among them, but promising that anyone who follows divine guidance will not go astray or suffer. Those who turn away from God’s remembrance, however, will have a life of hardship and be raised blind on the Day of Resurrection, as a consequence of ignoring God’s signs. This exchange illustrates the consequences of obedience and disobedience, and the enduring themes of guidance, repentance, and accountability.

The Surah reflects on past nations destroyed for their defiance, urging people to learn from the ruins they pass by. The delay of punishment is explained as God’s mercy, due to a prior divine decree and a fixed term, rather than an absence of justice.

The Prophet is counseled to be patient in the face of his opponents’ words and to worship God at all times of day and night, for spiritual satisfaction. He is advised not to be distracted by the fleeting allure of worldly wealth and status enjoyed by some, as these are tests, and God’s provision is both better and longer-lasting.

The Surah instructs the Prophet to enjoin prayer on his family and community, assuring him that God is the true provider and that the ultimate success is for those who are righteous. The demand from skeptics for more miracles is addressed: they have already received clear evidence from prior scriptures. If these people were destroyed before the Prophet’s arrival, they would have protested that they lacked a messenger; now that a messenger has come, each party must wait to see the outcome, and in the end, it will become clear who was rightly guided.

In summary, Sūrah Ṭā Hā weaves together themes of divine revelation, the unity and mercy of God, prophetic mission and struggle, the consequences of belief and disbelief, the centrality of prayer and remembrance, stories of earlier prophets, the dangers of idolatry and worldly attachment, the reality of resurrection and judgment, and the promise of forgiveness for the penitent. It reminds the reader that God’s guidance is continual and that those who embrace it will find purpose, security, and ultimate reward, while those who reject it will face hardship and regret, both in this life and the next.

Sūrah al-Anbiyā’ (“The Prophets”) is a Makkan surah that addresses a wide range of themes, including the reality of divine revelation, the fate of previous nations, the unity and sovereignty of God, the lives of earlier prophets, warnings about the Day of Judgment, and reminders of God’s mercy. It was revealed at a time when the Prophet Muḥammad (peace be upon him) and his followers were facing intense denial and ridicule from the Quraysh and other Makkan polytheists.

The surah opens by declaring that the reckoning for humanity is fast approaching, yet most people persist in heedlessness, distracted and turning away from the message. Even when new revelations come, the disbelievers are indifferent, treating them as mere entertainment rather than guidance. They dismiss the Prophet’s warnings, privately accusing him of being nothing more than a human, or even claiming he is practicing magic, and they question whether people should pay attention to someone like him.

The Prophet is instructed to reply that God is fully aware of every utterance in the heavens and the earth — nothing escapes His hearing or knowledge. In response, the disbelievers speculate that the revelation consists of confused dreams, or that Muḥammad has fabricated it, or that he is a poet. They demand miraculous signs similar to those shown by previous messengers, but they overlook the fact that none of the communities destroyed before them believed when faced with such signs, so why would they be different?

The surah emphasizes the humanity of all messengers: God only sent human prophets who ate food and were mortal. If the doubters are unsure, they are told to consult the “people of the message” (those with earlier scriptures). God always fulfilled His promises to His messengers, saving them and their followers, while destroying the wrongdoers. The Qur’an is presented as a Book in which the people’s own story and destiny are mentioned, urging them to reflect.

The destruction of past unjust societies is recounted: when they finally sensed God’s punishment, they tried to flee, but angels told them to return to their homes and former comforts for questioning. In their despair, they admitted their wrongdoing, but their pleas continued only until they were utterly annihilated, likened to a field of crops mown down or a fire extinguished. The surah clarifies that the heavens and earth were not created in vain or for play; if God had wanted mere amusement, He could have found it without creation. Instead, God uses truth to destroy falsehood, and those who invent lies about Him are warned of ruin.

The surah asserts God’s absolute ownership and majesty. All beings in the heavens and earth belong to Him. The angels — those nearest to God — are never arrogant, nor do they tire of glorifying Him day and night. Human beings are asked whether they have taken earthly deities who can resurrect the dead. The surah points out that if there were any gods besides Allah, the universe would fall into chaos. God is utterly transcendent, not subject to question about His actions, but all others will be questioned.

The oneness of God is further established. The Prophet is told to challenge the idolaters to bring any proof for their beliefs. The Qur’an is not only a message for the current audience but also a confirmation of the messages brought by earlier prophets. Every messenger preached the same core message: “There is no deity except Me (God), so worship Me.” The surah refutes the claim that “the Most Merciful has taken a son,” explaining that those they consider divine (like angels or Jesus) are in fact honored servants of God, who act only by His command, cannot intercede except with His permission, and are themselves in awe of Him.

The surah draws attention to the signs of God in creation: the heavens and earth were once one mass, then separated; all living things were made from water. God placed mountains to stabilize the earth, carved paths through them, and made the sky a protective ceiling. Yet, people ignore these signs. God created the cycle of night and day, the sun and moon, each moving in their orbits. No human is granted immortality — even the Prophet will die, and everyone will eventually return to God, each soul tasting death and being tested in both hardship and ease.

The surah describes how the disbelievers mocked the Prophet, ridiculing him for criticizing their gods while they themselves rejected the very mention of the Most Merciful (al-Raḥmān). Human beings are described as impatient; God cautions them not to rush His signs or threatenings, as the reality of His promise will come suddenly and without escape. Those who mocked previous messengers were themselves overtaken by the punishments they belittled.

The surah questions who could possibly protect humanity, day or night, from the Most Merciful if He willed punishment. The idols people turn to cannot help themselves, let alone defend others. Yet, God’s mercy is evident in the worldly prosperity and long lives He has granted even to the deniers and their ancestors. God warns that He is gradually shrinking the land from its borders (possibly referring to losses, conquests, or diminishing influence), and asks if the disbelievers think they can prevail against Him.

The Prophet is instructed to declare that his warnings are based on revelation, but those who are spiritually deaf cannot hear the call. Even the slightest touch of God’s punishment would cause the deniers to admit their wrongdoing. God promises perfect justice on the Day of Resurrection: scales will be set to weigh every deed, no soul will be wronged in the slightest, and even a deed as small as a mustard seed will be accounted for.

The surah references earlier revelations given to Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron): scripture that served as a standard (criterion) and a light for the righteous, especially for those who revere their Lord unseen and are fearful of the coming Hour. The Qur’an is similarly described as a blessed message. The surah then turns to stories of earlier prophets to reinforce its messages.

Ibrāhīm (Abraham) is highlighted for his wisdom. He challenged his father and people about their devotion to idols, questioning why they worshipped what their ancestors did without reason. Despite their suspicion and accusations, Abraham declared that their Lord is the Creator of the heavens and earth, and he plotted to expose the futility of their idols. When his people left, Abraham smashed their idols except the largest, so they would question it. When confronted, Abraham pointed to the largest idol as the culprit, sarcastically inviting them to ask their gods if they could speak. They realized their inconsistency, admitting their own error, but soon reverted to stubbornness. Infuriated, they ordered Abraham to be burned, but God commanded the fire to be cool and safe for him, saving Abraham and leaving his enemies as the true losers.

Abraham and his nephew Lūṭ (Lot) were delivered to a blessed land. Abraham was given sons, Isḥāq (Isaac) and Ya‘qūb (Jacob), all made righteous and appointed as leaders, inspired to perform good deeds, uphold prayer, and give charity (zakāh). Lūṭ, too, was given wisdom and knowledge and was saved from the evil, rebellious people of his city, who were ultimately destroyed. Lūṭ was admitted to God’s mercy for his righteousness.

The narrative continues with Nūḥ (Noah), who called on God and was saved, along with his family, from the great flood, while his people, who denied God’s signs, were drowned. Dāwūd (David) and Sulaymān (Solomon) are mentioned for their just judgment in a case involving sheep damaging a field; Solomon’s understanding of the matter is especially praised, though both were granted wisdom. David was given the miracle of the mountains and birds joining him in glorifying God and was taught the craft of making armor. Solomon was given control over the wind, which traveled at his command to a blessed land, and over jinn (supernatural beings) who dived for him and did various tasks, all under God’s watch.

The surah then recounts Ayyūb (Job), who prayed to God in distress and was relieved of his suffering, receiving his family and even more as a mercy and a lesson for worshippers. Ismā‘īl (Ishmael), Idrīs (Enoch), and Dhul-Kifl are all praised for their patience and righteousness, being admitted to God’s mercy.

The account of Yūnus (Jonah), referred to as “the man of the fish,” is told: he left his people in anger, thinking God would not decree hardship for him, but in the darkness (of the night, sea, and belly of the fish), he repented, proclaiming God’s oneness and his own error. God answered his plea and rescued him, making his story an example for believers. Zakariyyā (Zechariah) is remembered for praying for a child and being granted Yaḥyā (John), with his wife’s condition improved — both were devoted to good deeds and humble worship.

Maryam (Mary), who guarded her chastity, is recalled as a sign for all peoples: God sent His spirit (the angel Gabriel) to her, resulting in the miraculous birth of her son (Jesus), making both a sign for the world.

The surah then draws all these stories together, declaring that this religion is one religion, and God is the only Lord to be worshipped. Yet, people have divided themselves in matters of faith, but ultimately all will return to God. Those who do righteous deeds while believing will have all their efforts acknowledged, with God’s angels recording their deeds.

For those communities destroyed by God, return is forbidden until the apocalyptic events occur, including the unleashing of Ya’jūj and Ma’jūj (Gog and Magog), who will swarm from every elevation. At that time, the true promise (the Resurrection) draws near, and the disbelievers will be seized with horror, regretting their heedlessness and admitting their wrongdoing.

The surah contrasts the fate of the disbelievers — who, along with their false gods, will be fuel for Hell, eternally suffering — with that of the righteous, who will be completely removed from the torment, never hearing its sound, enjoying whatever their souls desire, and being greeted by angels with the glad tidings of the Day they were promised. The greatest terror will not sadden them.

The Day of Resurrection is described as the moment when God will fold up the heavens like a scroll of records, just as He began the first creation, He will repeat it — a promise He will unfailingly fulfill. The surah references earlier revelations, such as the Psalms, which foretold that God’s righteous servants would inherit the land (interpreted here as Paradise).

The surah closes by reaffirming that the Qur’an is a clear message for those who worship. The Prophet Muḥammad is told that he has been sent only as a mercy to all worlds. He is to proclaim the oneness of God and invite all to submit to Him. If people turn away, his duty is to deliver the message impartially; only God knows when the promised events will occur. God knows every spoken word and secret, and the Prophet acknowledges his lack of knowledge about whether God’s delay is a test or a temporary enjoyment for the people.

The surah ends with the Prophet’s prayer: “My Lord, judge between us in truth. Our Lord is the Most Merciful, whose help is sought against the lies you attribute [to Him].” This closes al-Anbiyā’ by bringing together its themes of prophetic mission, divine mercy, the fate of deniers, the unity of revelation, the reality of the resurrection, and the ultimate vindication of God’s truth.

Sūrah al-Ḥajj (“The Pilgrimage”) opens with a powerful warning to all humanity about the coming of the Last Day, the Day of Judgment. It urges everyone, not just believers, to be mindful of their Lord, emphasizing the unparalleled horror and chaos of the final Hour. The surah paints a vivid scene: even the most devoted mothers will forget their children, and pregnant women will miscarry from sheer terror. People will appear as if they are drunk, overwhelmed by fear, but it is the severity of God’s punishment that causes this state. This introduction sets the tone for the rest of the surah, grounding all its themes in the reality and seriousness of the Hereafter.

The surah then addresses the phenomenon of people who debate or argue about God without knowledge, blindly following rebellious devils. It explains that those who turn to such evil influences are led astray, ultimately to punishment in the Fire. This section highlights the danger of arrogance, ignorance, and following baseless speculation or tradition instead of clear guidance.

To address doubts about resurrection and the Hereafter, the surah gives a logical argument based on human development: God created people from dust, then a sperm-drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, some formed and some unformed. Each stage is under God’s control, with each life and death occurring by His will. The surah reminds listeners that God revives the dead earth with rain, producing lush growth—an analogy for resurrection. The point is that the Creator who brings life from inert matter and revives barren earth is fully able to resurrect the dead.

The surah insists that God is the ultimate reality (“the Truth”), fully capable of raising the dead, and that the coming of the Hour is certain. God will resurrect all who are in their graves. It repeats the condemnation of those who argue about God without any real knowledge, warning that such people act arrogantly, seeking to turn others away from the path of God. These people deserve disgrace in this world and severe punishment in the Hereafter, not as an injustice, but as a consequence of their own actions.

The surah describes a type of person who “worships God on the edge”—someone whose faith is shallow and conditional. If good comes their way, they are content; if trials hit, they abandon faith, losing both worldly and spiritual benefit. Such people turn to powerless beings or idols instead of God, seeking help from things that cannot benefit or harm them. The surah mocks the irrationality of this, stating their chosen “protectors” are useless and even more likely to harm than help.

By contrast, those who believe and act righteously are promised entry into gardens beneath which rivers flow—a common Qur’anic description of Paradise (Jannah). God does whatever He wills, and His support for His chosen messenger is certain, regardless of the opposition’s frustration or anger.

The surah explains that the Qur’an was revealed as clear, decisive verses, and that guidance is ultimately in God’s hands. On the Day of Judgment, God will resolve all disputes among various religious groups—Muslims, Jews, Sabeans, Christians, Magians (Zoroastrians), and polytheists—since He is witness over everything.

The universality of God’s authority is further emphasized: everything in the heavens and earth, including celestial bodies, mountains, trees, animals, and many humans, prostrate to Him (willingly or by nature).
