It reiterates the concept of creation and recreation, stating that both are equally easy for God. Allah is described as having the highest attributes and being supremely powerful and wise. To illustrate the irrationality of associating partners with God, a parable is offered: just as people would not accept that their servants should share equally in their own wealth, it makes no sense to claim that others share in God’s dominion or divinity.

Despite these clear arguments, many people follow their own desires blindly, without knowledge. The Surah states that those who have been left to stray by Allah cannot be guided by anyone else, and they will have no helpers. Therefore, the call is issued: turn wholeheartedly towards the true religion, following the fiṭrah (innate, primordial nature) upon which Allah created humanity. This fiṭrah is a natural inclination to monotheism and righteousness, and the Surah warns against corrupting it by introducing changes or divisions in religion. The correct way is to repent, fear Allah, establish regular prayer, and avoid both polytheism and religious sectarianism, which lead to fragmentation and false security in group identity.

The Surah describes the human tendency to turn to God in times of crisis but to revert to polytheism or ingratitude when relief comes. Some people deny Allah’s favors and blessings, claiming they have other sources of help or authority, but the Surah challenges them to produce any proof for such claims. It notes the fickleness of human nature: people rejoice at good fortune but despair at setbacks, failing to recognize that both prosperity and adversity are under Allah’s control. The wise understand that Allah can expand or restrict provision as He wills, and that both are signs for those who have faith.

Social and ethical guidance is also present. The Surah commands giving to needy relatives, the poor, and travelers, declaring this as the path to success for those seeking Allah’s approval. It distinguishes between selfish financial practices—such as usurious transactions (riba, often interpreted as interest or exploitative gain)—which do not bring true blessing, and charity (zakāh), which is given sincerely for God’s sake and is rewarded many times over.

The Surah returns to the theme of monotheism and the futility of associating partners with Allah. It points out that none of the false gods or partners attributed to Him have any share in creation, providence, or resurrection. Allah alone creates, provides, causes death, and brings life. The Surah then states that corruption and disorder have spread on land and sea due to what humans have done, and that people are allowed to taste the consequences of their actions in this life so that they might return to righteousness.

The Surah encourages reflection on history: people are invited to travel and observe the ruins of earlier civilizations that rejected monotheism and the prophets sent to them. Most of these past peoples were polytheists, and their destruction serves as a warning. The Surah urges people to return to the correct way before a Day comes from Allah that cannot be averted—the Day of Judgment—when humanity will be divided according to faith and deeds. The consequences of disbelief and righteousness are made clear: each person bears responsibility for their own choices, and the reward for belief and good deeds is out of Allah’s bounty.

The Surah emphasizes Allah’s merciful signs in nature, such as the winds that precede rain (which brings life to the earth and allows ships to sail, facilitating travel and commerce). These are reminders to be grateful. The Surah ties these natural phenomena to the broader theme of divine mercy and power. It then recalls the stories of previous messengers who came with clear evidence, and the pattern that followed: those who rejected them faced divine retribution, and God’s support for the believers was guaranteed.

The cycle of rain is described in detail as a metaphor for resurrection: Allah sends winds, forms clouds, and sends down rain to revive dead earth, bringing joy to people who were previously in despair. This renewal of life after barrenness is likened to how Allah will resurrect the dead. Yet, human gratitude is fleeting; if a destructive wind ruins their crops, people often fall into disbelief and ingratitude.

The Surah then addresses the limits of prophetic guidance: the Prophet cannot make the spiritually “dead” hear, nor those who have turned away in stubbornness, nor can he guide those who are blind to the truth. Only those who believe and are open to God’s signs benefit from the message and become Muslims (those who submit to God). The Surah describes the stages of human life—weakness in infancy, strength in youth, and weakness again in old age—underscoring Allah’s knowledge and power over all aspects of creation.

On the Day of Judgment, those who denied the truth will experience regret and confusion, claiming they only stayed in the world a short time, while the knowledgeable and faithful will correct them, stating that they remained until the appointed day of resurrection. On that day, excuses and pleas for mercy will be of no use to those who wronged themselves by rejecting faith.

In its conclusion, the Surah reflects on the comprehensive nature of the Qur’an, which contains many parables and examples to guide people. Yet, for some, no matter what sign is given, they persist in denial and accusation of falsehood. This stubbornness is described as a condition where Allah “seals” the hearts of those who lack true knowledge and openness, preventing them from perceiving the truth.

The Surah ends by addressing the Prophet Muḥammad directly, urging him to be patient and steadfast. It reassures that Allah’s promise is certain and true, and that the doubts and skepticism of those who lack conviction should not disturb or unsettle him. The ultimate victory belongs to truth, and the Surah closes with a call to perseverance in the face of adversity, faith in divine promise, and trust in the unfolding of God’s plan.

Sūrah Luqmān opens with the disjointed Arabic letters “Alif, Lām, Meem,” a literary feature found at the start of several Qur’anic chapters, whose precise meaning is known only to God. The Surah then immediately declares that what follows are verses from a “wise Book”—the Qur’an—presented as a source of guidance and mercy specifically for those who do good. These “doers of good” are characterized by their commitment to ritual prayer (ṣalāh), regular charity (zakāh), and their firm conviction in life after death. The Surah states that such people are truly guided by their Lord and will ultimately be successful.

In contrast to these righteous individuals, the Surah warns about a group of people who indulge in “amusement of speech”—a phrase interpreted by many commentators as referring to frivolous, distracting, or misleading stories, entertainment, or arguments designed to divert others from God’s way. Such individuals do so without knowledge and mock sacred teachings. The Surah sternly warns that these people will receive a humiliating punishment. When God’s verses are recited to them, they respond with arrogant indifference, acting as if they are deaf, and so they are threatened with painful retribution.

The Surah then reassures believers: those who have faith and act righteously are promised the “Gardens of Pleasure” (Jannah), where they will live forever. This is presented as a true promise from God, who is described as both “Exalted in Might” and “Wise.” The Surah turns attention to the wonders of creation, inviting listeners to reflect on the heavens, which are upheld without visible pillars, the firmly anchored mountains that stabilize the earth, the diversity of living creatures, and the rain that brings forth every kind of noble plant. This is all attributed to God’s creative power, and the Surah challenges doubters to show anything that other powers have created, making clear that such skeptics are in manifest error.

The narrative then shifts to the figure of Luqmān, from whom the Surah takes its name. Luqmān is not described as a prophet, but as a wise man whom God endowed with wisdom. Luqmān is instructed to be grateful to God, and it is explained that gratitude benefits the person who practices it, while God Himself is independent of all needs and praiseworthy regardless of human response. The Surah recounts Luqmān’s advice to his son, emphasizing the greatest sin: associating partners with God (shirk), which is called a “great injustice.”

The Surah then presents a universal command regarding parents: God has enjoined people to care for their parents, highlighting the mother’s particular hardship in pregnancy and nursing. Children are called to gratitude toward both God and their parents, though the ultimate return is to God. However, if parents urge their children to commit shirk (i.e., to associate others with God), the children are not to obey in this matter, but are still instructed to treat them kindly in everyday life and to follow the path of those who repent to God. Ultimately, God will judge everyone’s actions.

Continuing Luqmān’s advice, the Surah teaches that even the smallest wrong—something as tiny as a mustard seed, whether hidden inside a rock or anywhere in the universe—will be brought forth by God, who is described as “Subtle and Acquainted.” Luqmān counsels his son to establish prayer, advocate for what is right, forbid what is wrong, and exercise patience over life’s difficulties—qualities described as deserving of strong resolve.

Luqmān’s guidance continues with ethical advice on humility and self-control. He warns against arrogance—turning one’s cheek in contempt toward others or striding boastfully—and advocates a moderate, humble manner of walking and speaking. Speaking too loudly or harshly is discouraged, with the unpleasant braying of donkeys offered as a metaphor for offensive speech.

The Surah then invites all people to reflect on God’s generosity: everything in the heavens and the earth has been made of service to humanity, and God’s favors—both visible and hidden—are abundant. Yet, some people still argue about God without any knowledge, guidance, or divine scripture. When advised to follow God’s revelation, such people often cling to inherited traditions, even if these lead to destruction—reminded by the rhetorical question: would they persist if Satan himself was leading them toward the “Blaze” (Hellfire)?

The Surah highlights the virtue of submitting oneself wholly to God while doing good, describing this as grasping “the most trustworthy handhold,” an unbreakable support. All matters ultimately return to God. Those who reject faith will not harm the Prophet Muḥammad personally; their return is to God, Who knows all inner thoughts and intentions. Disbelievers may enjoy temporary worldly benefits, but ultimately, they will face severe punishment.

The Surah points out that even the polytheists of Arabia would acknowledge God as the Creator of the heavens and earth if asked, but their understanding remains incomplete. True praise belongs to God alone, who owns everything in existence and needs nothing from creation. The Surah then uses a powerful metaphor to describe the infinite nature of God’s words, wisdom, and decrees: if every tree on earth were made into pens and the sea, replenished by seven more, served as ink, God’s words would still not be exhausted. This underscores God’s limitless might and wisdom.

The Surah affirms that creating and resurrecting all of humanity is as easy for God as creating a single soul—His power is absolute, and He is all-hearing and all-seeing. The daily cycles of night and day, the movement of the sun and moon, and all natural phenomena are described as being under God’s control, further emphasizing His intimate awareness of everything people do.

The Surah points out the falsity of worshiping anything besides God, declaring that only God is the Truth, while all else invoked is falsehood. The ability of ships to sail at sea, made possible by God’s favor, is presented as another sign for those who are patient and grateful. In moments of crisis, such as storms at sea, even those who usually neglect God turn to Him sincerely; yet, once delivered to safety, many quickly forget and revert to disbelief. The Surah notes that only the treacherous and ungrateful reject such clear signs.

The Surah concludes with a universal warning to humanity: be mindful of God and the coming Day of Judgment, when no family ties will be of any help—neither father nor son can benefit the other. God’s promise of the Last Day is real, and people are cautioned against being deceived by the allure of worldly life or by Satan, “the Deceiver.”

The final verse articulates the limits of human knowledge and the absolute knowledge of God. Only God knows when the Hour (the Last Day) will occur, sends down rain, knows what is in the wombs, and is aware of every soul’s future deeds and the place of its death. This verse summarizes the Surah’s themes of humility, submission, and trust in divine wisdom, affirming that God alone is “Knowing and Acquainted” with all things.

In summary, Sūrah Luqmān weaves together guidance on belief in God’s oneness, proper worship, gratitude, familial duties, righteous conduct, humility, and recognition of God’s signs in creation. It warns against arrogance, heedlessness, and blind adherence to tradition at the expense of truth. By drawing on the wisdom of Luqmān and the realities of the natural world, the Surah invites listeners to a life of faith, ethical action, and awareness of ultimate accountability before God.

Sūrah as-Sajdah (The Prostration) is a Meccan chapter of the Qur’an, revealed during a period when the Prophet Muhammad and his followers faced intense opposition and skepticism from their community. The surah opens with the mysterious disjointed Arabic letters "Alif, Lām, Meem," which, as with other similar openings in the Qur’an, signal the divine origins of the message and challenge listeners to reflect on its meaning. Immediately, the surah asserts that it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds, leaving no room for doubt about its authenticity or its source.

The surah then addresses the accusations of Muhammad’s contemporaries, who claimed he had fabricated the Qur’an. It firmly rejects this allegation, insisting the message is the truth from God, sent to warn a people who had not previously received a messenger for some time. The implication is that this warning is an act of mercy, giving people the chance to be guided before it is too late.

Next, the surah turns to theological foundations. It describes God as the creator of the heavens, the earth, and everything in between, accomplishing this creation in six days before establishing Himself above the Throne—a metaphor for His supreme authority. The surah emphasizes that there is no protector or intercessor besides God, urging people to remember their dependence on Him alone.

The surah describes God’s ongoing governance of the universe: He manages all affairs from the heavens to the earth, and those affairs return to Him in a day that is described as equivalent to a thousand human years, highlighting both His transcendence over time and the limited nature of human understanding. God is described with attributes of knowledge (of both the unseen and the witnessed), might, and mercy.

The narrative then shifts to the origins of humanity. God is said to have perfected all creation, beginning the creation of the human being from clay and then continuing human progeny from a "despised liquid," referring to semen. God shaped human beings and breathed into them of His spirit, endowing them with faculties such as hearing, sight, and intellect. The surah laments that despite these gifts, people are seldom grateful.

The surah addresses the skepticism of those who deny resurrection, questioning how it is possible for humans to be re-created after disintegration in the earth. The surah responds that their real issue is disbelief in meeting their Lord. It asserts that the Angel of Death will inevitably take every soul, and all will be returned to God for judgment.

The surah then paints a vivid picture of the disbelievers' regret on the Day of Judgment. The wrongdoers will stand with heads bowed, pleading for another chance to return to the world and do good, claiming certainty in the truth. However, God’s decree is final: if He had willed, everyone would have been guided, but His word has been established that Hell will be filled with both jinn and humans who reject faith.

As a result, those who ignored the warning of the Hereafter are told to "taste" the punishment, as they are now forgotten just as they forgot their meeting with God. This punishment is described as eternal, and it is tied directly to the misdeeds they committed in life.

The surah contrasts the behavior and fate of true believers with that of the disbelievers. True believers are those who, when reminded of God’s signs, respond with humility, falling in prostration and glorifying their Lord without arrogance. They are described as people whose sides "part from their beds"—meaning they rise at night for prayer, supplicating to God with both fear and hope, and they are generous with what God has provided for them.

The reward for such faithful people is described as beyond human comprehension: "no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for eyes." This emphasizes the unique and unimaginable reward awaiting those who believe and act righteously.

The surah explicitly states that believers and defiantly disobedient people are not the same. The righteous will reside in the Gardens of Refuge (Paradise, "Jannah"), as a reward for their deeds, while those who disobeyed will find their abode in the Fire (Hell). Whenever the latter try to escape, they will be returned and told to taste the punishment they once denied.

The surah introduces the concept of “the nearer punishment” in this world, which may refer to trials, calamities, or disasters that befall people before the ultimate punishment of the Hereafter. This serves as a warning and a chance for people to repent before facing the greater punishment.

The surah asks rhetorically who could be more unjust than someone who, when reminded of God’s revelations, turns away. Such people are warned of God’s retribution, reinforcing the gravity of deliberate rejection.

The narrative briefly references the story of Mūsā (Moses), affirming that God gave him the Scripture (the Torah) as guidance for the Children of Israel. The Prophet Muhammad is reassured not to doubt God’s ability to bring about a meeting (possibly meaning the meeting with Moses in the Hereafter or the truth of Moses’ story). Among the Israelites, God appointed leaders who guided by His command, but only when they were patient and certain of God's signs.

The surah underscores that ultimate judgment of disputes among the Children of Israel—and, by extension, all people—will occur on the Day of Resurrection. Human differences and ambiguities will be resolved by God’s perfect justice.

The surah points out the evidence of past destroyed generations, whose ruins the contemporaries of Muhammad pass by. These should serve as signs and warnings, yet many fail to reflect or heed the lessons.

Similarly, the surah draws attention to a sign in the natural world: the cycle of rain and barren land coming to life, producing crops for humans and their livestock. This is presented as a clear demonstration of God’s power to resurrect the dead, yet many remain blind to such signs.

The surah notes the demand of skeptics who ask when the promised “conquest” or decisive event will occur, challenging the Prophet to produce the punishment or victory he warns of. The surah responds that, on the day when God’s judgment arrives, belief at that moment will not benefit the disbelievers, nor will they be given respite.

In its closing, the surah instructs Muhammad to turn away from the persistent rejecters and wait, for the decisive moment will inevitably come. The disbelievers, too, are waiting—whether for vindication or punishment—so the outcome will be settled by God in due time.

In summary, Sūrah as-Sajdah combines powerful theological affirmations about God’s sovereignty, creation, and justice with urgent warnings about the consequences of disbelief and heedlessness. It contrasts the attitudes and destinies of believers and deniers, using examples from history, signs in nature, and vivid descriptions of the afterlife to urge reflection, humility, and gratitude. Throughout, it reinforces the inevitability of resurrection and divine judgment, while also emphasizing that true guidance and ultimate reward are in God’s hands alone.

Sūrah al-Aḥzāb (“The Confederates” or “The Combined Forces”) is a Madinan chapter of the Qur’an, revealed during a time of great social, political, and military upheaval for the early Muslim community. Its verses address a range of issues: the authority and example of the Prophet Muḥammad, social reforms, the conduct of the Prophet’s household, the events of the Battle of the Trench (al-Aḥzāb), the relationship between Muslims and non-Muslims, rules related to adoption and marriage, and core theological warnings and promises.

The Surah begins by instructing the Prophet Muḥammad to remain conscious of God (Allāh), to avoid following the suggestions of disbelievers and hypocrites, and to adhere closely to divine revelation. The Prophet is reminded to have unwavering trust in God, who alone is sufficient to manage all affairs. This introduction emphasizes the Prophet’s unique responsibility and the centrality of divine guidance.

The Surah then tackles several key social reforms. It rejects pre-Islamic concepts such as the notion of a person having “two hearts,” the practice of declaring one’s wife as “unlawful” in the manner of one’s mother (a practice called ẓihār), and the custom of treating adopted sons as blood relatives in matters of lineage and inheritance. Instead, adopted children are to be identified by their biological fathers, but where this is unknown, they are still to be treated as brothers in faith and valued members of the community. This introduces a new ethical approach to family structure and personal identity, while affirming God’s forgiveness for past mistakes made in ignorance.

The Prophet’s relationship to the believers is also redefined. He is described as being “more worthy of the believers than themselves,” and his wives are given the honorific status of “mothers of the believers,” indicating their revered position. Blood relatives, however, are designated as primary heirs, though kindness to close associates through bequests is permitted. These rules are described as having been decreed in the “Book” (divine decree).

The Surah next references the solemn covenant taken from a select group of prophets—Noah (Nūḥ), Abraham (Ibrāhīm), Moses (Mūsā), Jesus (ʿĪsā), and Muḥammad—highlighting the continuity and seriousness of their roles. God will question the truthful about their fulfillment of this covenant, while those who reject faith are warned of a painful punishment.

The narrative then shifts to the historical context of the Battle of the Trench, when a coalition of tribes and opponents (the “Confederates”) besieged Madinah. The believers are reminded of God’s favor: He sent a wind and unseen forces (interpreted as angels) to aid the Muslims and disperse their enemies. The psychological state of the besieged community is described—the fear, uncertainty, and severe testing faced by the believers, as well as the doubts and defeatism expressed by the hypocrites and weak-hearted.

The Surah describes how some hypocrites tried to abandon the defense, making excuses or urging others to retreat, contrary to their earlier pledges to stand firm. God exposes their insincerity and warns that fleeing from death or battle would not grant them any real benefit; no one can protect them from God’s will. The contrast between those who shirked their duties and those who fulfilled their promises is made clear: the latter are praised for their steadfastness, while the former are criticized for their cowardice and duplicity.

Special mention is made of the conduct of the Prophet as an example (“an excellent pattern”) for all believers, especially those who hope in God and the Last Day. The Surah highlights how true faith is reinforced in times of trial, with believers responding to adversity by reaffirming their trust in God’s promises. Some fulfilled their vows by sacrificing their lives, while others awaited similar opportunities, but all remained true to their commitments. God will reward the sincere and punish or forgive the hypocrites as He wills.

God’s ultimate intervention is recounted: He repelled the Confederates with no material gain for them, affirming His power and sufficiency as the protector of the believers. The Surah also describes the fate of the Banu Qurayẓah, a Jewish tribe in Madinah who had allied with the Confederates. They were brought down from their fortresses, some were killed, and others were taken captive. The Muslims inherited their lands and properties, as well as other lands yet to be conquered, by God’s decree.

The attention then turns to the private lives of the Prophet and his wives. The Prophet is instructed to offer his wives a choice: if they desire worldly life, he will release them graciously; if they choose God, the Messenger, and the afterlife, they will receive a great reward. The wives are reminded that their position carries both higher expectations and greater consequences: any public immorality will be punished doubly, while obedience and righteousness will bring double reward and noble provision.

The wives of the Prophet are told that they are not like other women. Accordingly, they are advised to be modest in speech, to avoid drawing the attention of those with ill intentions. They are urged to remain within their homes, avoid pre-Islamic displays of beauty, perform prayers, give charity (zakāh), and obey God and His Messenger. God’s intention is to purify the Prophet’s household completely. The wives are also reminded to reflect on the verses and wisdom being recited in their homes.

In a broader statement, the Surah enumerates the qualities that earn God’s forgiveness and great reward: faith, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, chastity, and constant remembrance of God, for both men and women. This egalitarian affirmation highlights that men and women alike have access to spiritual reward based on their character and deeds.

The Surah then asserts that when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, no believing man or woman has the right to disagree or choose otherwise. Disobedience in such cases is described as clear error.

The Surah addresses a sensitive episode involving Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, the Prophet’s adopted son. The Prophet advised Zayd to keep his wife, Zaynab, though he secretly knew God would decree otherwise. When Zayd divorced her, God commanded the Prophet to marry Zaynab, breaking the taboo against marrying the ex-wife of one’s adopted son. This was to demonstrate that adopted sons do not have the same legal status as biological sons, removing any cultural discomfort for believers. The Prophet is reassured that he should feel no embarrassment regarding what God has commanded, as such precedents existed among previous prophets.

The Surah reaffirms the Prophet’s status: Muḥammad is not the biological father of any of his male followers, but he is the Messenger of God and the final (“seal”) of the prophets. This establishes his unique position and the finality of prophethood in Islamic belief.

Believers are then urged to remember God frequently and glorify Him throughout the day. God and His angels bestow blessings upon the believers, leading them from darkness to light and promising them peace and a noble reward in the Hereafter.

The Prophet’s mission is summarized: he is sent as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, an inviter to God by His permission, and a radiant source of guidance. Believers are assured of God’s great bounty.

The Surah repeats the command to ignore the pressures of disbelievers and hypocrites, not to harm them, and to trust in God. This is a call to patience and reliance on divine support in the face of opposition.
Legal guidance is given regarding believing women who are divorced before consummation of marriage: no waiting period (ʿiddah) is required, but they must be given provision and a gracious release.

The Prophet is granted particular allowances in marriage: he may marry those women to whom he has given their dowries, captives granted by God, certain close relatives who emigrated with him, and any believing woman who offers herself in marriage if he wishes. These privileges are exclusive to the Prophet, in contrast to the general rules for other believers, and are intended to ease his burdens. However, he is not permitted to marry more women thereafter or to exchange his existing wives except for captives.

Social etiquette is addressed: believers should not intrude on the Prophet’s home, should only visit when invited, and must not linger for idle conversation. When they need to ask something of his wives, they should do so from behind a screen, to maintain modesty and purity of heart. Marrying the Prophet’s wives after him is strictly forbidden, as it would be a grave offense in God’s eyes. God’s knowledge encompasses all hidden and revealed matters.

The rules for the Prophet’s wives and, by extension, believing women, are further clarified: they may interact freely only with close male relatives and other women, and they must remain mindful of God’s awareness of all things.

The Surah highlights the special status of the Prophet: God and His angels confer blessings upon him, and believers are urged to do the same by invoking blessings and peace upon him. Those who insult God or His Messenger are cursed and face humiliating punishment in this world and the next.
The Surah condemns those who harm innocent believing men and women by slander or false accusation, declaring it a manifest sin.

The Prophet is instructed to tell his wives, daughters, and the believing women to draw their outer garments (jilbāb) around themselves when in public. This command is intended to help them be recognized as respectable women and to protect them from harassment. God is forgiving and merciful even in these matters.

The Surah warns that if hypocrites, those with sick hearts, and rumor-mongers in Madinah do not desist from their behavior, God will empower the Prophet against them, leading to their expulsion or even destruction—consistent with God’s unchanging way of dealing with persistent evil in previous communities.

In response to questions about the timing of the Last Day (the Hour), the Prophet is told to say that only God knows its timing, and it may be near. Disbelievers are warned of eternal punishment in the Fire, longing in vain for obedience to God and His Messenger, and blaming their leaders for their fate. They ask for double punishment for those who led them astray.

The believers are cautioned not to follow the example of those who maligned Mūsā (Moses), as God vindicated him and he was honored in God’s sight. Instead, they are urged to speak justly and to fear God, which will lead to their deeds being accepted and their sins forgiven.

The Surah closes with a profound allegory: God offered the “Trust” (interpreted as free will, religious responsibility, or the covenant with God) to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains, but they declined due to its gravity. Humanity accepted it, despite being prone to injustice and ignorance. This sets the stage for the final reckoning: God will punish hypocrites and idolaters, but will accept the repentance of sincere believers. The Surah ends by affirming God’s constant forgiveness and mercy.

Sūrah Saba' (The Chapter of Sheba) opens by praising Allah, stating that all praise belongs to Him alone—both for everything in the heavens and the earth, as well as for the Hereafter. Allah is described as all-wise and fully aware, highlighting His comprehensive knowledge and perfect judgment. The Surah immediately establishes Allah as the owner and maintainer of all creation, deserving of praise now and forever.

It continues by emphasizing Allah’s complete knowledge over all things—He knows everything that enters the earth (such as seeds, rain, or buried bodies) and what comes out of it (like plants or the resurrected dead). Similarly, He is aware of everything that descends from the sky (rain, revelation) and what ascends (prayers, deeds). This establishes Allah as merciful and forgiving, but also as possessing detailed, encompassing knowledge over the universe and its cycles.

The Surah then addresses a key theological debate: the reality of the Hour (the Day of Judgment). The disbelievers deny its coming, mocking the idea of resurrection. The Prophet is instructed to affirm categorically that the Hour will indeed come, swearing by his Lord. Allah’s knowledge is so precise that not even the smallest particle, or anything smaller or greater, escapes His record. This serves to assure believers of accountability and to warn deniers that nothing is missed or insignificant in Allah’s judgment.

The Surah establishes the purpose of this knowledge and the coming Judgment: so that those who believe and do good deeds will be rewarded with forgiveness and a generous, honorable provision, while those who actively oppose Allah’s revelations will face a severe, humiliating punishment. The Surah highlights that individuals of knowledge recognize the truth of the Quran and its guidance toward the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, in contrast to the ignorant or stubborn rejecters.

The Surah turns to the arguments of the disbelievers, who ridicule the Prophet’s message by questioning the plausibility of bodily resurrection after total decay. They accuse the Prophet of either fabricating lies about Allah or being mad. The Surah counters by stating that it is the rejecters of the Hereafter who are truly astray and destined for punishment, not the Prophet. It then points to the natural world—the heavens and the earth—urging people to reflect on their surroundings and realize Allah’s power to overturn their existence at any moment, such as causing the earth to swallow them or sending down destruction from the sky. These are reminders for anyone who turns to Allah in humility.

The Surah introduces narratives of previous prophets and peoples to illustrate Allah’s favor, human ingratitude, and the consequences of both. It begins with Dāwūd (David), to whom Allah gave special blessings: the mountains and birds would echo his praises, and iron was made soft for him, enabling him to craft armor with precision. David and his family were enjoined to do righteous deeds and show gratitude, with a reminder that Allah observes all actions.

The narrative continues with Sulaymān (Solomon), who was given command over the wind (which could carry him vast distances in a short time) and access to a flowing spring of molten copper—a valuable resource. Solomon was also served by jinn (supernatural beings), who built for him grand structures and objects. However, any jinn that disobeyed faced severe punishment. These gifts were a test for Solomon’s household to work gratefully, with the note that only few servants of Allah are truly grateful.

The story of Solomon’s death is recounted as a lesson on the limits of even supernatural knowledge. The jinn, who thought Solomon was alive and continued laboring under his rule, only realized his death after a creature (thought to be a termite) gnawed through his staff, causing his body to fall. This revealed that the jinn did not possess knowledge of the unseen, dispelling myths about their power and knowledge.

The Surah then recounts the story of the people of Saba' (Sheba), an ancient and prosperous community in Yemen. They were blessed with fertile land and two lush gardens, enjoying a comfortable and forgiving existence. They were urged to enjoy their provisions and show gratitude to Allah, but they turned away and became ungrateful. As a result, Allah sent a devastating flood that destroyed their gardens, replacing them with barren land and bitter fruit—symbolizing the loss of blessings due to ingratitude and disbelief.

The people of Saba’ had also been granted an extensive network of towns and safe travel routes between their homeland and other blessed cities (possibly referring to the trade routes to Syria and Palestine). Their lifestyle was made easy and secure, but they arrogantly requested that the distances between their journeys be increased, desiring hardship out of boredom or pride. As punishment, their civilization was scattered, their story becoming a cautionary tale. This is presented as a sign for those who are patient and grateful, showing that prosperity is maintained through gratitude and humility.

The Surah shifts to a broader reflection on human susceptibility to the influence of Iblīs (Satan). The people of Saba’ (and, by extension, humanity) confirmed Iblīs’s assumption that most people would follow him, except for a minority of true believers. The Surah clarifies, however, that Iblīs has no real authority over humans; his influence is only a test to distinguish those who believe in the Hereafter from those who doubt or reject it. Allah is the ultimate guardian over all matters.

The Surah returns to the central theme of monotheism, challenging the idea of other beings or deities having any share in Allah’s power or authority. It instructs the Prophet to ask the idolaters to call upon their supposed gods, pointing out that these beings have no ownership, partnership, or assistance in the heavens or earth. Even intercession is not possible except by Allah’s permission, and when the reality of the Hereafter dawns, all will recognize Allah’s exclusive authority, and their claims will be exposed as false.

The argument continues with rhetorical questions: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth? The answer is unequivocally Allah. The Prophet is instructed to assert that either he or the disbelievers is upon the right guidance, but the matter will be settled when Allah brings everyone together for judgment. Each will only be responsible for their own deeds, and Allah alone will decide between them in truth.

The Surah emphasizes the universality of the Prophet Muhammad’s mission, stating that he was sent to all of humanity as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner. Yet, most people remain ignorant or unresponsive to this message. The disbelievers demand to know when the promised punishment or judgment will occur, to which the response is that it is set for a specific Day from which no one can escape or delay.

The Surah then describes the arguments that will erupt between different groups of disbelievers on the Day of Judgment. The oppressed will blame the arrogant leaders for leading them astray, while the leaders will retort that the followers were themselves at fault. The reality is that both groups will regret their choices and face the consequences of their actions, with shackles placed on the necks of the disbelievers as a symbol of their bondage to wrongdoing.

The narrative points out a recurring pattern in human history: every time a messenger was sent to a community, it was typically the wealthy and powerful who openly rejected the message, boasting in their numbers and material success as evidence of divine favor. They claimed immunity from punishment because of their prosperity. The Surah rebuts this by clarifying that provision and wealth are distributed by Allah as He wills, and these things do not bring anyone closer to Him. What matters is faith and righteous action; those who excel in these will be doubly rewarded and dwell in secure, elevated stations in Paradise.

In contrast, those who stubbornly oppose Allah's revelations and seek to frustrate His message will be consigned to the punishment. The Surah reiterates that Allah is the true provider, able to expand or restrict sustenance according to His wisdom. Whatever is spent in His cause will be compensated, and He is the best of providers, encouraging charity and trust in divine recompense.

On the Day of Judgment, Allah will question even the angels about whether they were worshipped by humans. The angels will declare their innocence and clarify that it was the jinn whom most people worshipped in ignorance. On that day, no one will be able to help or harm another; the wrongdoers will be told to taste the punishment they had denied.

The Surah addresses the accusations made against the Prophet Muhammad when he recites the Quran’s clear signs. The disbelievers claim he is trying to turn people away from their ancestral traditions and accuse him of fabrication or sorcery. The Surah notes that these people had not even received earlier scriptures or messengers, so their rejection is not due to inherited religious knowledge, but willful denial.

It reminds the Meccan audience that previous nations, who were far greater in power and resources, were destroyed when they rejected Allah’s messengers. Their downfall serves as a stark warning to those who respond to the Quran with similar disbelief.

The Prophet is instructed to advise the people to reflect sincerely and independently about his message, either individually or in pairs, to see that he is not mad but a sincere warner before a severe punishment comes. He makes clear that he seeks no payment from them; his reward is with Allah alone, affirming his sincerity and the selflessness of his mission.

The Surah concludes with a powerful affirmation: Allah brings forth the truth, and falsehood is powerless—it cannot initiate or restore anything. The Prophet clarifies that if he were misguided, the harm would be upon himself, but if he is rightly guided, it is through Allah’s revelation, who is always near and responsive.

The final verses depict the scene of the Hereafter, when the disbelievers will be seized with terror and regret, desperately wishing to believe, but too late for repentance. They had previously denied and speculated arrogantly about the unseen, but now the chance for faith and salvation is lost. Just as happened with previous peoples, a barrier is set between them and what they desire—namely, salvation or a return to the world to make amends—because in this life they were in persistent doubt and denial.

Throughout, Sūrah Saba’ weaves together themes of divine knowledge, gratitude, the reality of resurrection, the futility of idolatry, the lessons from earlier prophets and civilizations, the consequences of arrogance and ingratitude, and the ultimate justice of Allah. It invites reflection, patience, and gratitude, warning that worldly success does not guarantee divine favor, and reminding that true success lies in faith, righteous deeds, and preparation for the Hereafter.

Sūrah Fāṭir (The Originator) opens with an expression of praise for Allah, who is described as the Creator of the heavens and the earth. The Surah highlights Allah’s unique power by mentioning that He alone created the angels, assigning them as messengers with varying numbers of wings, and that He continually increases His creation as He wills. This introduction establishes Allah’s absolute capability and creative authority over all things.

The Surah emphasizes Allah’s absolute control over mercy and blessings. Whatever mercy or bounty Allah grants to people, no one can withhold; and whatever He withholds, no one can release. Allah is described as both Mighty and Wise, underscoring both His power and His wisdom in how He distributes His favors. The early verses urge all humanity to remember Allah’s favors, especially His role as the sole provider of sustenance from the heavens and the earth. The rhetorical question—can anyone other than Allah provide for you?—reinforces the theme of monotheism, warning against being misled into associating partners with Him.

The Surah addresses the Prophet Muhammad’s (peace be upon him) mission, reassuring him that denials and rejections are not new; previous messengers were also denied. Yet, all matters ultimately return to Allah. The Surah warns all people not to be deceived by the transient nature of worldly life or by Satan (Shayṭān), who is explicitly identified as a persistent enemy. Satan’s only goal is to draw people into the ranks of those destined for Hellfire (the Blaze). The Surah contrasts the fate of disbelievers, who face severe punishment, with believers who do good deeds, for whom forgiveness and a great reward are promised.

The text explores the idea that some people are so deluded by the seeming goodness of their own misdeeds that they believe themselves to be right. It clarifies that Allah, in His wisdom, may allow people to go astray or to find guidance according to His will. Muhammad is told not to grieve excessively over those who reject faith, as Allah is fully aware of their actions.

The Surah presents a parable from nature to illustrate resurrection: Allah sends winds that move clouds, bringing dead land back to life with rain. This natural process is likened to how Allah will resurrect the dead. It is a reminder that resurrection is not beyond Allah’s power, just as reviving lifeless earth is not.

Allah is described as the source of all honor and power. Anyone seeking true dignity should turn to Him, for all honor ultimately belongs to Him. Good words and righteous deeds ascend to Him; in contrast, those who plot evil will face severe punishment, and their schemes will ultimately fail.

The Surah briefly reviews the stages of human creation: from dust, then a drop of sperm, and then into pairs (male and female). It emphasizes Allah’s complete knowledge of every stage of life, including conception, birth, aging, and death. Every lifespan is precisely recorded with Allah, and none of it is difficult for Him.

A reflection on the diversity in creation follows: the Surah compares two types of seas—one fresh and sweet, the other salty and bitter. From both, people derive benefits, such as edible seafood and ornaments. Ships travel across these waters, allowing people to seek Allah’s bounty. These contrasts are meant to inspire gratitude.

The Surah points to further signs of Allah’s power: the alternation of night and day, the subjugation of the sun and moon, each running its course for a set period. These cosmic phenomena are evidence of Allah’s sovereignty. In contrast, those invoked as partners alongside Allah possess no power, not even as much as the thin membrane inside a date seed. These false gods cannot hear, respond, or intercede, and on the Day of Resurrection, they will disavow those who worshipped them.

Humanity’s dependence on Allah is highlighted. All people are in need of Allah, while He is entirely free of need and worthy of all praise. Allah has the power to replace humanity with a new creation if He wills, and this would not be difficult for Him.

The Surah teaches personal responsibility: no one can carry another’s sins, even if they are closely related. Guidance and warning are only effective for those who are mindful of Allah in the unseen and who pray regularly. Self-purification benefits the individual, and all ultimately return to Allah.

The Surah uses a series of contrasts to illustrate the difference between faith and disbelief: the blind and seeing are not equal, nor darkness and light, nor shade and heat, nor the living and the dead. Allah alone can make people truly “hear” His message, but Muhammad cannot force understanding upon those who are spiritually dead. The Prophet’s role is to warn, just as previous warners were sent to every nation.

The Surah reminds listeners that the pattern of denial and rejection is ancient: previous communities denied their messengers even after receiving clear proofs and divine scriptures. Those who rejected faith faced severe consequences—a warning to those who now deny Muhammad.

The Surah turns back to nature, observing how Allah sends down rain, producing fruits of varying colors, and how even the mountains display a spectrum of colors. Similarly, people, animals, and livestock are diverse in appearance. The Surah notes that only those with knowledge truly fear Allah, recognizing the signs of His power and mercy in creation.

The Surah describes the qualities of the righteous: those who recite Allah’s Book, pray regularly, and spend in charity both publicly and privately. For these people, Allah promises a never-failing reward, full recompense, and even more out of His bounty. Allah is both forgiving and appreciative of their efforts.
The revelation given to Muhammad is confirmed as the truth, matching and affirming earlier scriptures. Allah is fully aware of all His servants’ actions and intentions.

The Surah describes the inheritance of the divine scripture. Allah has chosen certain servants to inherit the Book, and among these are three categories: those who wrong themselves (by sin), those who are moderate in their faith, and those who are foremost in good deeds by Allah’s permission. This is described as a great favor. For these people, the reward is described in vivid terms: everlasting gardens (Jannah, Paradise), adorned with gold, pearls, and silk garments, where sorrow, fatigue, and weariness are banished.

In contrast, the fate of disbelievers is bleak: the fire of Hell awaits them. Death will not come to relieve them, and the punishment will not be lessened. When they beg for another chance, they are reminded that they had ample opportunity and warning in their previous lives, but ignored them. Now there is no help for the wrongdoers.

Allah’s complete knowledge is again stressed: He knows the unseen aspects of the heavens and earth, as well as the secrets within people’s hearts. He has made humanity inheritors of the earth, but those who persist in disbelief only increase their own loss and Allah’s disfavor.

The Surah challenges the logic behind polytheism. It asks the disbelievers to present any evidence that their so-called partners have created anything in the heavens or the earth, or that they have any share in divine authority. Lacking any proof, their mutual promises are described as nothing but delusion.

The Surah reinforces that Allah alone sustains the heavens and the earth. If He were to withdraw His support, nothing could keep creation intact. Despite humanity’s frequent straying, Allah is described as Forbearing and Forgiving.

The Surah notes that some people had previously sworn that if a warner came to them, they would be more guided than others. However, when Muhammad came, their response was only to grow more stubborn and hostile, due to arrogance and plotting evil. But evil plotting only rebounds upon their own people. Allah’s system is unchanging; the fate of rejecters will always be the same.

The Surah invites reflection on history: previous peoples who were mightier than the current audience were destroyed when they defied Allah. No power in the heavens or earth can prevent Allah’s will. He is always knowledgeable and capable.

The Surah closes with a message of divine mercy: if Allah were to punish humanity immediately for their wrongs, nothing would be left alive, but He gives people time. When the appointed time comes, Allah will hold everyone to account, for He is always watchful over His servants.

In summary, Sūrah Fāṭir weaves together theological affirmations of Allah’s creative power, warnings against disbelief and arrogance, reminders of personal responsibility, appeals to recognize divine signs in the natural world, descriptions of the fate of both believers and disbelievers in the Hereafter, and affirmations of the Prophet Muhammad’s role as a warner in a long line of messengers. The Surah repeatedly urges gratitude, humility, and reflection, drawing on both the wonders of creation and the lessons of history to persuade its audience of the truth and urgency of its message.

Sūrah Yā Seen, a chapter of the Qur’an often called “the heart of the Qur’an,” opens with the mysterious disjointed letters “Yā, Seen,” a device found in several chapters whose precise meaning remains uncertain but serves to catch the listener’s attention. The chapter then immediately swears by the “wise Qur’an,” emphasizing the profound wisdom embedded in the revelation and affirming that the Prophet Muhammad is indeed one of God’s messengers, guided by a straight and true path. The surah stresses that this revelation comes from God, who is both powerful and merciful, and that Muhammad’s mission is to warn a people whose ancestors had not been warned for a long time, leaving them heedless of divine guidance.

The surah then acknowledges that, despite the Prophet’s efforts, most people will not believe because the divine decree against them has already come into effect due to their persistent refusal to accept guidance. Their hearts and minds are described metaphorically as being shackled and barricaded; they are unable to see or comprehend the truth, no matter how clearly it is presented. For such people, it makes no difference whether they are warned or not—they will not believe. But the surah clarifies that those who are open to the message and fear God even without seeing Him will benefit: they can look forward to God’s forgiveness and a generous reward.

The chapter then reminds listeners that God brings the dead to life and records everything people do, both their deeds and their legacies—nothing escapes His knowledge. All actions are meticulously recorded in a “clear register,” reinforcing the idea of divine justice and ultimate accountability.

To illustrate the consequences of rejecting God’s messengers, the surah presents a parable: the story of a town to which God sent multiple messengers. Initially, two messengers are sent and denied; a third is sent to reinforce their message. The townspeople reject them, accusing them of lying and being nothing more than ordinary humans. The messengers insist on their divine commission and clarify that their duty is merely to deliver the message clearly. The townspeople respond with threats and blame the messengers for bringing bad omens. The messengers counter that the people’s misfortune is due to their own actions, not the messengers’ reminder.

Amidst this confrontation, a man from the farthest part of the city rushes in to support the messengers. He urges his people to follow the messengers, pointing out their sincerity and that they ask for no payment. He questions why he should not worship the One who created him, warning that false gods can neither help nor protect if God wills harm. He openly declares his faith in the Lord and invites others to listen. The narrative shifts abruptly: the man is told to “enter Paradise,” and he expresses a wish that his people could know how he has been forgiven and honored by God.

The surah notes that God did not deploy angelic armies to punish the town after this man’s death; instead, their destruction came with a single, overwhelming blast. This sudden annihilation underscores God’s power and the finality of His judgment. The passage laments humanity’s tendency to ridicule messengers and reject every warning, noting that many earlier generations were destroyed and will not return—but all will ultimately be gathered before God for judgment.

The surah then turns to signs of God’s power and mercy in the natural world, urging people to reflect. It describes how lifeless earth is revived, producing grain for food, and how gardens of palm trees and grapevines flourish through God’s provision of water. These blessings, which humans did not create themselves, are cited as reasons for gratitude. God is praised as the One who creates all pairs in nature—plants, animals, and even things unknown to humans—highlighting the diversity and balance in creation.

Further, the alternation of night and day is given as a sign: the coming of darkness as daylight is withdrawn, and the precise movement of the sun and moon in their orbits, each following a set course. These cosmic phenomena are presented as evidence of God’s wisdom and control. The surah also recalls how God saved people in laden ships (alluding to Noah or general sea travel) and created similar means of transport for later generations. It reminds that if God willed, He could cause people to drown, but He mercifully spares them for a time.

Despite these signs and warnings, the surah observes that people persistently turn away. When told to be mindful of their past and future—potentially meaning the consequences of their actions—they ignore the advice. When urged to share their wealth, the disbelievers retort that if God wanted certain people fed, He would have done so Himself, implying that helping the needy is pointless. This attitude is denounced as misguided and arrogant.

The surah then addresses the skepticism of those who question when the promised Day of Judgment will arrive. It warns that the end will come suddenly, with a single blast that overtakes people while they are preoccupied with worldly disputes. When the moment arrives, there will be no opportunity to warn others or return home; all will be resurrected and hasten from their graves to face God.

On the Day of Judgment, people will be bewildered, questioning who has raised them from their “sleeping place.” It will be clarified that this is the fulfillment of God’s promise and the truth spoken by the messengers. The resurrection will happen in an instant, and everyone will be brought before God for judgment. On that day, no one will be wronged; everyone will be compensated precisely for their deeds.

The surah describes the joy of the people of Jannah (Paradise): they and their spouses will recline in comfort, enjoy abundant fruits, and receive whatever they wish. They will also be greeted directly with “Peace” from the Merciful Lord, signifying ultimate acceptance and contentment.

In stark contrast, the guilty are commanded to stand apart. God reminds humanity of His ancient command not to worship Satan—who is a clear enemy—but instead to worship God alone, which is the straight and true path. Yet, many people have been led astray. The surah identifies Hell as the promised destination for those who denied the truth, and they will endure its punishment as a direct result of their choices.

The surah vividly describes the reckoning: people’s mouths will be sealed, but their hands and feet will testify about their actions, making self-deception or denial impossible. God notes that, if He willed, He could have deprived them of sight or movement, further emphasizing His power and their dependence on His mercy. The process of aging is also cited as a sign: as people grow old, their faculties decline, reminding them of their vulnerability and the cyclical nature of life.

The chapter then clarifies a misconception about Prophet Muhammad: he was not taught poetry, nor is the Qur’an poetry. Rather, it is a clear message meant to warn those who are spiritually alive and to confirm the condemnation of those who persist in disbelief. The surah continues to highlight God’s favors: He created livestock for humans, made them tame and useful for riding, food, and other benefits. Despite such clear blessings, people are often ungrateful.

The surah criticizes those who set up false gods, believing they will help, when in fact these idols can neither assist nor defend themselves. The surah reassures the Prophet not to be saddened by people’s words, for God knows both what they reveal and what they conceal.

The surah then reflects on human arrogance: people forget their humble origin from a mere drop of fluid and yet become argumentative and defiant toward their Creator. Some skeptics mock the idea of resurrection, asking who could revive decayed bones. God instructs the Prophet to reply that the One who created them in the first place can surely re-create them, for He knows all creation intimately.

As further evidence of God’s creative power, the surah mentions how He brings fire from green trees—a reference to the process by which Arabs made fire from certain green woods—demonstrating the wonders embedded in natural processes. If God created the vast heavens and earth, recreating humans is certainly within His power. His command is effortless: when He wills something, He simply says “Be,” and it is.

The surah concludes by exalting God as the sovereign over all things, reminding that ultimately, everyone will return to Him. The final verse encapsulates the surah’s overarching themes: divine power, resurrection, human accountability, the futility of disbelief, and the certainty of return to God. Throughout, the surah weaves together warnings, reminders, signs in creation, parables of past peoples, and vivid depictions of the afterlife to persuade, warn, and awaken its audience to the reality of God’s message.

Sūrah aṣ-Ṣāffāt (“Those Who Line Up”), revealed in the middle to late Makkan period, opens with a series of oaths. It swears by the angels, described as lining up in rows, driving the clouds, and reciting the divine message. These images establish the order, discipline, and purposefulness of creation, as well as the authority of the message being delivered. The Surah immediately emphasizes the unity and uniqueness of God (Allah): He is the sole Lord of the heavens, the earth, and everything in between, as well as the Lord of all points of sunrise. The beauty of the sky is highlighted through its adornment with stars, which also serve as a protective barrier against rebellious devils (shayāṭīn), preventing them from eavesdropping on the exalted assembly of angels. When these devils attempt to steal a fragment of heavenly speech, they are repelled and pursued by blazing flames, ensuring that the purity of divine revelation is safeguarded.

The Surah then confronts those who doubt resurrection and the afterlife. It challenges the disbelievers to consider whether their own creation is more difficult than what God has already made, reminding them that humans were created from sticky clay, a humble origin. Despite this, the Prophet Muhammad is astonished by their mockery and disbelief. When reminded of the truth, they ignore it; when shown signs, they dismiss them as magic. They openly question the possibility of resurrection after death, both for themselves and their ancestors, to which the Prophet is commanded to assert that not only will resurrection occur, but the deniers will be in a state of humiliation.

The Surah vividly describes the Day of Judgment: a sudden, overwhelming event where the dead will be resurrected with a single blast. The disbelievers, now realizing the reality, will lament, recognizing it as the Day of Recompense they had denied. On this day, angels will be commanded to gather together the wrongdoers, their associates, and all that they used to worship besides Allah, leading them towards Hell. Before entering, they will be questioned about their deeds and why they failed to help one another. In utter submission and helplessness, they will turn on each other, blaming one another for misguidance. Their leaders will admit that they had no real authority and that each individual is responsible for their own rebellion. Both leaders and followers will share in the punishment, a principle that underscores the personal accountability of every soul.

The Surah notes the core reason for their punishment: arrogance and refusal to accept the message of monotheism, dismissing the Prophet as a “mad poet.” It affirms that Muhammad has brought the truth and confirmed the essential message of previous prophets. The Surah insists that people will be repaid only for their own deeds—except for the “chosen servants of Allah,” who are exempt from this fate.

In contrast to the punishment of disbelievers, the Surah paints a detailed picture of reward for the chosen servants. They will receive a defined provision, including fruits and honor, in lush gardens of delight (Jannah, or Paradise). There, they will recline on thrones facing each other, enjoying pure and delicious drinks that do not intoxicate or harm, and the companionship of beautiful, devoted partners described with poetic imagery. The atmosphere is one of peace, enjoyment, and mutual conversation. A notable parable follows: a resident of Paradise recalls a former companion who doubted resurrection. He is shown his companion suffering in Hell and acknowledges that, but for God’s grace, he might have shared that fate. The people of Paradise then express gratitude that death and punishment are now behind them, recognizing their immense good fortune.

The Surah contrasts the bliss of Paradise with the suffering of Hell. It introduces the tree of zaqqūm, a dreadful food for the wrongdoers in Hell, growing from its depths and bearing fruit as repulsive as devils’ heads. Those consigned to Hell will eat from it, filling their bellies, then drink scalding water, and return again and again to torment. This punishment is linked to their uncritical imitation of their forefathers in error, a theme emphasized throughout Makkan revelation. The pattern of following ancestral tradition blindly, despite repeated warnings and the example of destroyed nations before them, is condemned.

The narrative then shifts to a series of brief accounts of earlier prophets and their peoples, illustrating the fates of those who responded to or rejected the divine message. The story of Nūḥ (Noah) is recounted: he called upon God, was saved along with his family from disaster, and his descendants became the survivors. Noah is honored with the greeting of peace, and his story is set as a model reward for the righteous. His people, however, were drowned.

The Surah then moves to Ibrāhīm (Abraham), a direct descendant of Noah, who approached his people and father with a sound heart, questioning their worship of idols. Abraham cleverly distances himself from their rituals, feigning illness, then destroys their idols to expose their powerlessness. When confronted, Abraham challenges their logic in worshipping what they themselves create, rather than the Creator. In response, they attempt to execute him by fire, but God saves him and humiliates his enemies. Abraham subsequently prays for righteous offspring, and God grants him a patient son.

The Surah recounts the famous episode where Abraham, following a divine dream, prepares to sacrifice his son (widely understood in Islamic tradition to be Ismaʿīl, or Ishmael). The son willingly submits, but at the last moment God intervenes, declaring Abraham’s trial fulfilled and ransoming the child with a great sacrifice. This event is presented as a supreme test of faith and obedience and is commemorated with the greeting “Peace upon Abraham.” Abraham is further blessed with the good news of another son, Isḥāq (Isaac), who is also to be a prophet. God’s blessing extends to both sons’ descendants, though among them are both righteous and sinful individuals.

The Surah next turns to Mūsā (Moses) and Hārūn (Aaron). God recounts saving them and their people from great hardship (the oppression of Pharaoh), granting them victory, and bestowing upon them the revealed scripture (the Torah). Their guidance on the straight path and their enduring honorable mention are affirmed, and they too are recipients of peace and reward.

The Surah briefly mentions Ilyās (Elias or Elijah), a prophet sent to warn his people against the worship of Baʿl, a pagan deity. Ilyās calls them to worship the true Creator, the Lord of all ancestors, but is mostly rejected, with only the chosen servants saved from punishment. Ilyās, like the other prophets, is honored with the greeting of peace and recognized as a true believer.

The narrative continues with Lūṭ (Lot), who, along with his family (except his wife), is rescued from destruction as punishment befalls his people for their persistent wrongdoing. The ruins of Lot’s people are presented as a visible sign for the Quraysh, who pass by them on their trade routes yet fail to take heed.

The story of Yūnus (Jonah) follows. Jonah flees his mission, ends up on a heavily laden ship, and, after drawing lots, is thrown overboard. Swallowed by a great fish, Jonah is in a state of blame, but through his prayers and glorification of God, he is saved and released onto shore in a weakened state. God causes a gourd vine to shelter him, and Jonah is eventually sent to a community of more than one hundred thousand people, who believe and are granted prosperity for a time.

The Surah then returns to the theological issues of the Quraysh. It challenges their beliefs about God having daughters (contrasting with their preference for sons) and the claim that angels are female. These assertions are dismissed as lies and baseless speculation. The Surah challenges them to provide any scriptural evidence for these ideas, exposing them as groundless fabrications. It also addresses a related pagan claim: that God and the jinn share lineage. The Surah states that even the jinn know such claims are false and will result in punishment.

The Surah, at various points, makes exceptions for the “chosen servants of Allah” (ʿibād Allāh al-mukhlisīn), emphasizing that they are free of such blasphemous beliefs and will be saved from punishment. The Surah makes it clear that no idol or false deity can mislead anyone except those already destined for Hell. The angels themselves are quoted, affirming that each has a designated role and position, and that they line up in order and continually glorify God, highlighting their obedience and the order of the unseen world.

The Surah recalls the objections of the disbelievers, who claimed that if only they had received a message like earlier peoples, they would have been God’s chosen servants. However, when the Qur’an was actually revealed to them, they rejected it. The inevitability of God’s promise is reaffirmed: His messengers will be victorious and His servants will ultimately prevail. The Prophet is counseled to be patient and to wait, as the disbelievers will soon witness the consequences of their actions when divine punishment arrives.

The Surah closes with a series of exaltations: God is declared far above any false descriptions attributed to Him. Peace is invoked upon all the messengers, and praise is offered to Allah, Lord of all worlds, encapsulating the Surah’s themes of monotheism, prophetic guidance, the reality of the afterlife, divine justice, and the ultimate triumph of truth.

Sūrah Ṣād opens with a single Arabic letter, “Ṣād,” followed by an emphatic statement about the Qur’an being a message full of reminder and guidance. The Surah immediately highlights the stubborn pride and discord of those who disbelieve in its message, noting that such arrogance is not new—many generations before the present audience also rejected divine warnings, only to be destroyed when it was too late for them to escape God’s judgment.

The Surah then describes the response of the disbelievers in Makkah to the Prophet Muhammad’s (peace be upon him) message: they are surprised and dismissive that a human “warner” has arisen from among their own people. They accuse him of being a magician and a liar, and mock his teaching of monotheism—specifically, his insistence that there is only one God, which they find strange and threatening to their traditional pagan beliefs. Their leaders encourage persistent defense of their ancestral gods and claim that monotheism is a novel fabrication, unheard of in their recent religious traditions. They question why Muhammad, out of all people, should be chosen for this message, but the Surah clarifies that their doubt is rooted in ignorance and that they have not yet experienced Divine punishment.

The Surah challenges the arrogance of the disbelievers by asking if they possess the treasures of God’s mercy, or dominion over the heavens and earth. If they truly had power, the Surah taunts, they could try to ascend to the heavens themselves, but in reality, they are nothing more than a doomed group destined for defeat, just like earlier communities who opposed God’s messengers.

Several destroyed nations are then listed as historical warnings: the people of Nūḥ (Noah), the tribe of ʿĀd, Firʿawn (Pharaoh) known for his oppressive reign, Thamūd, the people of Lūṭ (Lot), and the “companions of the thicket” (traditionally understood as the people of Madyan). Each of these groups denied their prophets, so God’s punishment was inevitable and justified upon them. The Surah warns that the current disbelievers should expect a similar fate, which will come suddenly and without delay—only a single blast (understood as the trumpet of the Day of Judgment) will suffice to end their respite.

The arrogance of the disbelievers is further illustrated by their mocking request for God to hasten their share of the punishment, demonstrating both their disbelief in accountability and their impatience. In response, the Prophet is instructed to remain patient in the face of their insults and to find solace by reflecting on the example of Dāwūd (David), who is described as a strong and devout servant of God, constantly turning to Him in repentance.

The Surah then recounts unique blessings given to David: the mountains and birds joined him in praising God, and he was given a strong kingdom, wisdom, and the ability to judge fairly. The narrative shifts to a particular incident involving two disputants who entered David’s private prayer chamber. They present a case: one brother has ninety-nine ewes (female sheep) and the other only one, but the wealthy brother wants to take the single ewe for himself. David rules in favor of the wronged brother, recognizing the general human tendency toward oppression except for those who believe and do good deeds—a group described as a minority.

David then realizes that this encounter was a test from God, prompting him to ask forgiveness and prostrate in repentance. God accepts his repentance, granting him nearness and an honorable place in the Hereafter. David is reminded of his role as God’s representative on earth, with the duty to judge justly and not let personal desires lead him astray—a warning that those who neglect justice and forget the Day of Judgment face severe consequences.

The Surah then shifts to a broader reflection on creation, stressing that the heavens, earth, and everything between them were not created in vain. Disbelievers who assume otherwise are warned of the Fire that awaits them. The Surah questions whether the righteous and the corrupt should be treated the same, or the God-fearing and the wicked be given equal standing—implying that divine justice makes clear distinctions between them.

The Qur’an is described as a “blessed Book” sent to Muhammad so that people may reflect on its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded. The Surah moves to another prophetic narrative: Solomon (Sulaimān), the son of David, is praised as an exemplary servant, devoted to God. An episode is recounted where Solomon is so captivated by his fine horses that he loses track of time and neglects remembrance of God, but then repents, demonstrating his humility and devotion.

Another trial faced by Solomon is alluded to, where a mysterious “body” is placed on his throne—interpreted by scholars as a symbol of a temporary loss of power or a personal test. Solomon then prays for forgiveness and requests a unique kingdom, unmatched by any after him. God answers by granting him control over the winds, the jinn (supernatural beings), and enormous wealth and power, with the ability to grant or withhold as he wishes. Yet, his true reward is nearness to God and an honorable place in the afterlife.

The Surah continues with the story of Ayyūb (Job), who endures severe suffering inflicted by Satan. Job calls out to God, who instructs him to strike the ground, producing a healing spring. God restores Job’s health and family, doubles his previous blessings, and approves of his patience. A specific incident is mentioned where Job, having made an oath in a moment of distress, is taught a gentle way to fulfill it without harm, highlighting God’s merciful accommodation. Job is praised as an outstanding, patient servant who consistently turned to God.

The Surah then recalls other prophets— Ibrāhīm (Abraham), Isḥāq (Isaac), Yaʿqūb (Jacob), Ismāʿīl (Ishmael), al-Yasaʿ (Elisha), and Dhū al-Kifl—each described as exceptional servants chosen for their spiritual strength and focus on the Hereafter. They are honored as outstanding in God’s sight, serving as reminders and examples for humanity.

The Surah moves to a depiction of the afterlife, contrasting the destinies of the righteous and the wicked. The righteous are promised beautiful gardens (Jannah, or Paradise), with open doors, luxury, abundant food and drink, and companions described as modest and of equal age—rewards that are everlasting and never diminish. This is the fulfillment of God’s promise to them for the Day of Judgment.

In contrast, the transgressors are warned of a terrible destination: Hell (Jahannam), where they will burn and suffer, forced to drink scalding water and endure various torments. The inhabitants of Hell will argue and reproach one another, blaming their leaders for leading them astray and wishing for double punishment upon those most responsible. They will express surprise at not seeing certain people whom they had mocked in the world, wondering if their ridicule was misplaced or if some trick of perception has hidden these people from them. God affirms that these disputes are a real feature of the afterlife.

The Prophet is then instructed to clarify his role: he is merely a warner, and there is no deity except Allah—the One, the All-Powerful, the Lord of the heavens and earth, and the Ever-Forgiving. He is to declare that the message he brings is “great news,” though many turn away from it. The Prophet himself had no prior knowledge of the heavenly disputes (among the angels) about the creation of Adam; he is only conveying what has been revealed to him.

The Surah recounts the story of Adam’s creation, when God announced to the angels His intention to create a human from clay and ordered them to prostrate to Adam after his soul was breathed into him. All the angels obeyed, except Iblīs (Satan), who refused out of arrogance, claiming superiority because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay. God rebukes Iblīs and expels him from Paradise, decreeing a curse upon him until the Day of Judgment.

Iblīs asks for a reprieve until the Resurrection, which God grants, specifying a known time. Satan then vows to mislead all of humanity except God’s chosen, sincere servants. God responds with a decisive statement: the truth is that Hell will be filled with Satan and all who follow him.

The Surah concludes with the Prophet reiterating that he seeks no payment or reward for delivering the Qur’an and is not seeking fame or prestige. The Qur’an is described as a universal reminder for all worlds, whose reality will become clear with time, even to those who currently reject it. The Surah ends with a subtle but firm warning that the truth of its message is inevitable and will be realized in due course.
